author: Brian Hioe
title: Endangered Eastern Grass Owl Habitat Threatened by Shalun Science Park
content:
ENVIRONMENTALISTS HAVE warned of the potential displacement of the Eastern grass owl as a result of the construction of the Shalun Science Park.

The Eastern grass owl is a critically endangered species in Taiwan, with its habitat including Tainan, Chiayi, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and it is Taiwan’s only owl species that nests in grasslands. After much effort by environmentalists to rebuild its habitat on the Dadu Mountain Plateau, the Eastern grass owl was found to have returned to central Taiwan earlier this year. It is thought that the Eastern grass owl disappeared from central Taiwan in the 1960s.

Environmentalists voiced concerns about the owl’s habitat at the second-stage environmental impact review, whose scoping session concluded on October 12th. The planned development zones “Parking 1” and “Industrial 1-2” would threaten the habitat of the Eastern grass owl, in that the current area is considered top-tier nesting grounds for the owl. As such, developers were urged to create habitats for the Eastern grass owl before construction. The Kaohsiung Science Park has been cited as an example of where development has already displaced the Eastern grass owl.

Science parks consume vast amounts of water and electricity. Nevertheless, it is common for local politicians to call for their development, with the view that this brings tech jobs to local populations. Likewise, with Taiwan increasingly central to the AI boom, in terms of providing the world with its supply of necessary semiconductors, this has led to a demand for facilities to keep up the pace–including not only semiconductor fabs themselves, but the facilities they need to keep running, such as power supply. And yet, as seen with the Eastern grass owl, this threatens the local environment.

Indeed, this proves another way in which the AI boom is reshaping Taiwan. While environmental destruction is commonplace with AI development, mostly along the lines of data centers and manufacturing, this can also occur with land acquisition–sometimes infringing on labor rights.

The relocation of Kuai Kuai from its current Taoyuan factory to Hsinchu, which is too far for the existing workers to commute, is due to the land the factory sits on being sold to a semiconductor company. Kuai Kuai’s owners were accused by striking workers, then, of having potentially acquired the land in order to sell it to semiconductor manufacturers, given that it is lucrative real estate. It is possible that land grabs by the semiconductor industry will become increasingly common in Taiwan, something that poses a risk not only to labor but also to the environment. This is to be seen.

Jake Johnson


Oct 30, 2026


 


Dockworkers in more than 20 countries—from

France

 to India to Greece—are withholding their labor on Friday to demand an end to Israel’s genocidal assault on

Gaza

 and highlight the role that commercial ports play in fueling deadly

militarism

 worldwide.


 


Organizers said the work stoppages, led by dockworkers’

unions

 at

113 ports across 22 countries

, would be the “largest coordinated port action ever,” easily surpassing the international day of action held in February. No Harbour for

Genocide

, a collective of

trade

workers

“A cargo refused in one port sails on to the next,” said No Harbour for Genocide. “Refused in every port, it stops, and the workers have enforced the embargo that governments announced and did not.”


 


In a

joint statement

Greece

An immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and the opening of safe corridor for

humanitarian aid

apartheid

Lebanon

solidarity

Cuba

 and

Venezuela

 and

Sudan

imperialism

 and we call for defend people’s sovereignty, resources, territorial integrity, peace with justice, and the right for resistance for self-determination.


 


Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops. We call on unions to strengthen vigilance, to inform workers, to expose the cargoes of war, and to organize mass collective resistance with all our rightful available means and our struggle.


 


An end to the

militarization

 of ports and critical

infrastructure

. Ports belong to the peoples and the workers. They are not bases for

NATO

, the USA or the EU, nor tools of shipowners and monopoly groups.


 


No to the war economy and armaments. The money must go to wages, collective agreements, health, education, social needs, and the protection of life and safety at work.


 


Health and safety measures in the workplaces. Not one worker dead for profits. An end to intensification, subcontracting, dangerous conditions, and employer arbitrariness.


 


Collective agreements with real wage increases, stable jobs with rights, a retirement policy with better pensions, and a reduction of working time. Technological developments, mechanization, automation, the use of AI and the development of ports must serve the needs of workers, and not lead to the intensification of work or the disappearance of their jobs.


 


“Our strength lies in organization. It lies in our unions, in general assemblies, in collective decisions, in solidarity among workers from different countries,” the unions said. “We, the workers in the ports, know very well that without us nothing moves. Without our hands, containers remain still, ships are not loaded, the war machines are blocked.”


 


Al Jazeera

noted

author: Daniel Aloc
title: Ganggang ni JL Burgos bilang salamin ng lipunan
content:
Natatangi ang karanasan ng mga batang lumalaki sa kanayunan, malayo sa kalunsuran na may madaling access sa teknolohiya. Sa pagitan ng pagpasok sa paaralan at paglalaro sa mga burol at parang—kabilang na ang paghahanap ng mga gagambang panlaban sa kapwa gagamba—unti-unti nilang natututuhan ang mga realidad ng mundong kanyang ginagalawan. May nananalo, may natatalo; may nambubully, at may napipilitan lumaban upang hindi na lamang manatiling api.

Ngunit paano kung ang mga larong kinalakihan nila ay naging daan upang maaga silang mamulat sa karahasang umiiral sa lipunan? Paano kung ang mga batang dapat sana ay malayang naglalaro ay maagang nahaharap sa dahas, takot, at pang-aabuso.

Ilan lamang ito sa mga tanong na sinisikap sagutin ng Ganggang, ang kauna-unahang full-length narrative film ni JL Burgos, na unang ipinalabas sa Cinemalaya noong Agosto. Nitong Oktubre 21 ko lamang ito napanood sa Cinematheque Centre Manila, na ngayo’y matatagpuan sa bagong tahanan nito sa Philippine Film Heritage Building sa Intramuros, bilang bahagi ng Pelikula ng Bayan: Cinemalaya 22.

Hindi na katakataka ang tema at paksang tinatalakay ng pelikula, lalo na’t ang gumawa nito ay isang filmmaker na matagal nang nakatuon sa usapin ng karapatang pantao. Bago ang Ganggang, nakilala na si Burgos sa mga dokumentaryong Portraits of Mosquito Press at Alipato at Muog (2024). Ang huli ay nagwagi ng Best Picture, Best Documentary, at Best Editing sa ika-48 Gawad Urian noong 2025.

Hindi isang bagong proyektong biglaang nabuo ang Ganggang kasunod ng tagumpay ng Alipato at Muog. Ayon kay Burgos, isinulat niya ang kwento noon pang 2019. Sa halip na talikuran ang mga isyung matagal na niyang tinalakay sa kanyang mga dokumentaryo, pinili niyang ilahad ang mga ito sa pamamagitan ng naratibo ng isang pelikula—sa lente ng mga batang hindi pa lubusang nauunawaan ang bigat ng mga puwersang humuhubog sa kanilang buhay.

Sa pelikula, sina Ilay (Kenneth “Butchoy” Vincent Mendoza), Ten-ten (Don Rishmond Cerbito), at Mel (Raine Dela Cruz) ay tatlong batang naging magkaibigan sa paghahanap ng gagambang panlaban sa gagamba ni Anton (Prince Nathaniel España), ang bully sa kanilang paaralan. May kanya-kanyang pinagmulan ang tatlong bata. Anak ng isang desaparecido si Ilay, anak ng magsasaka si Ten-ten, at anak na naman ng isang sundalo si Mel.

Sa unang tingin, ang Ganggang ay isang pamilyar na bahagi ng pagkabata sa maraming pamayanan sa bansa. May tuwa sa paghahanap ng gagamba at sa pananabik na makita kung alin ang mananaig. Ngunit isa itong alegorya ng isang lipunang tila nakondisyon nang maniwala na kailangang maglaban-laban ang mamamayan upang mabuhay.

Sa talkback at Q&A session matapos ang screening, ipinaliwanag ni Burgos ang kahulugan ng tunggalian ng mga gagamba. Hindi naman likas sa mga ito ang mag-away sa paraang nakikita sa laro; inilalagay sila ng tao sa sitwasyong kailangan nilang magpatayan. Katulad ng mga mamamayang napipilitang mag-unahan at maglaban sa isang sistemang pinaghaharian ng iilan.

Sentrong usapin ng pelikula ang militarisasyon sa kanayunan. Binabago ng presensya ng mga sundalo ang pang-araw-araw na buhay ng mga residente, kabilang ang mga guro at magsasakang itinuturing na mga miyembro o tagasuporta ng New People’s Army (NPA) dahil lamang sa kanilang mga paninindigan.

Bukod sa karahasan at paglabag sa karapatang pantao na iniuugnay sa estado, ipinakikita rin nito ang epekto ng karahasan sa mga bata at kanilang pamilya.

Mahalagang banggitin na ang ilan sa mga karakter at eksena sa pelikula ay hango sa mga tunay na tao at pangyayari.

Isa rito si Rebelyn, ang gurong karakter sa pelikula na hango kay Rebelyn Pitao, anak ni Leoncio Pitao, na mas kilala bilang Commander Parago ng NPA sa Davao. Noong 2009, dinukot si Rebelyn at natagpuan ang kanyang bangkay kinabukasan. Ayon sa ulat ng Commission on Human Rights, ang biktima ay may mga saksak sa dibdib at iba pang palatandaan ng matinding tortyur. Ang sinapit ni Rebelyn ay isang paalala na ang mga taong hindi naman aktwal na nakikidigma ay maaari pa ring maging target ng estado.

Ang plaka naman ng sasakyang ipinakikita sa unang bahagi ng pelikula ay kapareho ng plaka ng sasakyang ginamit sa pagdukot sa kapatid ng direktor na si Jonas Burgos sa isang mall sa Quezon City noong 2007. Hanggang ngayon, hindi pa natatagpuan si Jonas.

Hango rin sa mga tunay na pangyayari ang eksenang nire-red-tag ng isang opisyal ng militar ang gurong si Rebelyn at ang kaniyang mga kasama bilang mga rebelde …

author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and …

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. However, when I was conducting this research, I came across a number of findings that I want to share widely:

author: Omar Hassan
title: Ben Carroll’s ‘new direction’ for Victoria is towards the big end of town
content:
In his first statement released following the ousting of Jacinta Allan, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll promised “a new direction” for Victoria. So far, it’s been the longitudinal equivalent of prostrating yourself at the feet of the bosses and hoping for a better ride in the media. And it doesn’t feel that new.

Granted, Carroll came to office more determined than Allan to concede to each and every one of the right-wing attacks on the Labor government. He has distanced himself from the Big Build, and immediately announced a royal commission into the CFMEU, the key demand of the bosses and right wing who see an opportunity to strike a blow against unionism.

Carroll has also announced a softening of the land tax changes introduced by former premier Daniel Andrews, one of the few progressive taxation policies introduced in recent years. This is a signal to business and the wealthy that a Carroll government will not be expecting them to make sacrifices to reduce the state’s debt. 

But on many other issues, Carroll is more of the same. Crime is an example. The capitalist media’s constant focus on incidents of anti-social behaviour has created the impression that Victorians are living in an era of unprecedented violence and crime. Yet the crime rate is 

roughly the same

 as it was a decade ago, according to data drawn from the Victorian Crime Statistics Agency. 

Nevertheless, Caroll has announced a “zero tolerance” approach to crime, involving “less bail, more jail”. Not satisfied with their draconian “adult time for adult crime” laws introduced by Allan which target children as young as 13, Labor has promised a review aimed at legislating harsher sentences for young offenders. His government has also committed $150 million in new funding for expanded police and PSO numbers. The latter are being empowered to patrol in wider areas, including shopping malls.

Police are also being given the right to frisk people for knives anywhere at any time, despite a 2022 Griffith University review into a similar law in Queensland finding that there was “

no evidence

” that it deterred knife carrying or led to a reduction in violent offending. What the policy will definitely achieve is to expand the systematic harassment of youths from poor and migrant backgrounds.

To the extent there are real issues with anti-social behaviour and crime, much of it is driven by poverty, the housing crisis and lack of social services. According to the Council for Homeless Persons (CHP), the homeless population rose by 24 percent in the five years to 2021, the last census for which data is available. The perpetrators of this invisible crime are the developers and the banks, but most of all the Labor government, which is responsible for Victoria having the lowest proportion of public and community housing in Australia. The CHP also reported that the Victorian government slashed spending on social housing by 9 percent in the 2024–25 budget, despite having the largest number of people seeking emergency housing support. 

The Labor government is also demolishing every public housing tower in the city to make way for private development on lucrative inner-city land. The residents of these buildings have largely been dispersed to the outer suburbs, where housing is cheaper and services are woefully inadequate. 

In a similar vein, the government has failed to address the ballooning numbers of people seeking support in dealing with drug and alcohol problems. In May, the Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association reported there were 5,122 Victorians on daily waitlists for drug treatment services, a 115 percent increase since the pandemic. These are people who are actively seeking support, but 40 percent had not even been assessed. 

Insofar as there is youth crime, it can’t be separated from the conditions of life for many young people, and in particular the condition of schools. Too many, especially those in poor areas, are not adequately resourced, particularly when it comes to assisting students with special needs. It is a disgrace that we still lack full-time professional social workers and counsellors in every public school, and that it is incredibly difficult to get funding for support staff in classrooms without a disability diagnosis. The government prefers to lock kids up rather than support them to get an education.

Faced with these issues, the obvious answer is to increase funding to assist people in acute situations to find shelter, health care …

author: Syafiq Fadli, Cheong Huei Ting
title: States refuse to act on South East Asia’s transboundary haze
content:
The recent State of Global Air report published by the Health Effects Institute and published on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service website, identified Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania as the region with the fourth-highest death rates attributable to air pollution, at 100 deaths per 100,000 people.

The World Health Organization reports that “when inhaled, health-damaging pollutants including small particulates can penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing them to reach almost all organs within the body, including but not limited to cardiovascular, reproductive and metabolic systems, brain, liver and kidneys.”

The wildfires in parts of Indonesia, which started in early September, have impacted communities across South East Asia. Malaysian climate activists Syafiq Fadli and Huei Ting Cheong look at the origins of this toxic air pollution and why governments still refuse to take serious action to protect lives.

Transboundary haze has been a recurring environmental issue in Malaysia and the Southeast Asia region since the late 1990s, caused by slash-and-burn land clearing methods to cultivate palm oil plantations and a highly humid tropical climate with temperature fluctuations. It is a form of air pollution characterised by fine particles in the atmosphere that comprise pollutants such as smoke, dust, and industrial emissions, which combine with water vapour. This massive scale of air pollution has occurred so frequently it is now referred to as the “haze season”.

But this year’s haze has been extremely serious. It has been going on for about 2 months and no indication of stopping, further exacerbated by the El Niño weather system, which has brought drier conditions to the region. It is still treated as a “natural disaster”, however, ordinary people are suffering the consequences of actions by large agriculture companies, proven by countless studies and activists on the field.

Oil palms are not native to Malaysia or Indonesia, yet these two countries are at the heart of Southeast Asia’s palm oil empire, accounting for roughly 85% of global palm oil production. European colonial powers first introduced oil palms to the region as ornamental plants. However, as rubber markets declined after World War I, colonial plantation economies began shifting towards oil palm as a new profitable commodity, transforming vast stretches of land in Malaya and Indonesia into plantations.

This shift came at a devastating cost. Native plants, traditional food systems and self-sufficient ways of life were disrupted or destroyed to make way for commercial agriculture. Indigenous communities and local populations were displaced and subjected to exploitative labour systems, including indentured and contract labour, under colonial plantation regimes in the region. What was once a landscape shaped by diverse ecosystems and local livelihoods was increasingly reorganised around extraction and profit.

Today, the colonisers have left, but the plundering and destruction continues - this time by modern capitalist forces, driven by agribusinesses across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. Vast areas of biodiverse tropical rainforest in Malaysia and Indonesia have been cleared for palm oil plantations, contributing to severe biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and deforestation.

The fires and transboundary haze that plague the region are also linked to a complex web of corporate ownership, plantation concessions and business interests. Companies identified in reporting and investigations into plantation-related fires and land clearing include Malaysian firms and Indonesian plantation operators connected to Singapore-based business groups.

Examples include: PT Damai Agro Sejahtera — affiliated with Singapore-headquartered Bumitama Agri Ltd; and PT Arjuna Utama Sawit — identified as part of First Borneo Plantations, a plantation business with reported Singapore connections, and more.

The underlying pattern remains strikingly familiar: land and forests are treated as resources to be extracted for profit for the colonial powers back then and agribusinesses today, while indigenous communities, local livelihoods and the environment bear the consequences. When the profit is fully extracted, no compensation is given to the people, and barely any conservation efforts are made.

Such is the case with capitalism, where the world’s resources are exploited for the benefit of the few, while ordinary …

author: Editors
title: Turmoil in world politics: we have to rise to the challenges
content:
“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times ... it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.” The famous opening words of Charles Dickens novel,

A Tale of Two Cities,

 set in the Great French Revolution could equally apply to France and much of Europe today.

The best of times and spring of hope—the vibrant, months-long school student mobilisations and blockades that have drawn hundreds of thousands of French workers and university students onto the streets in solidarity. All in the face of savage police violence unleashed by President Emmanuel Macron’s government of the supposed moderate liberal centre.

Eventually, after weeks of foot-dragging, trade union leaders called a general strike for 5 November—a vital step forward and test for the rebellion.

It is not just France. A wave of protest inspired by the French students has swept Europe from Belgium to Portugal to Italy, where students and workers have long endured similar attacks on living standards and democratic rights, the rise of militarism and threatening fascist forces.

Spain has also been gripped by revolt over the cost of living and housing crisis sparked by the eviction of 87-year-old woman Maricarmen Abascal. The general strike called for 11 November is set to be the largest in Spain in the 50 years since the fall of General Franco’s fascist government.

But it’s also the worst of times—reflected in the scale of support for far-right forces internationally.

The majority of the French population sympathises with the protestors’ grievances over the cost-of-living, cuts to public services and education funding. Yet polls indicate Marine Le Pen of the fascist National Rally is set to decisively win April’s presidential elections. Le Pen leads the left’s Jean-Luc Melenchon 69 percent to 31 percent. 

Large sections of the capitalist class and its middle-class supporters are rallying behind National Rally as the “party of order” to crush resistance not just from unruly students but organised workers and impose harsh austerity measures to boost profits.

Similarly in Spain, the right-wing People’s Party backed by the fascist Vox seems set to defeat the discredited centre-left government in the 29 November elections on a program of wage cuts, mass public sector sackings and attacks on democratic rights.

Then there is Brazil. An inspiring wave of protests led by young people transformed the course of the elections ensuring the defeat of the far right’s Flavio Bolsonaro. Yet the increasingly violent far right shows no sign of being curbed. Ruling in the interests of Brazil’s capitalist class, Lula da Silva’s Workers Party disillusioned swathes of workers and the poor preparing the ground for the far right. And a re-elected Lula is not about to change course and mobilise workers in mass strike action to challenge the rich and powerful.

Politics worldwide has become much more polarised, the product of decades of neo-liberal attacks on workers’ living standards and increasingly authoritarian rule undermining the hold of parties of the centre-left and centre-right. The pattern is uneven, but in many countries it is the far right that so far has been the main beneficiary of the growing discontent.

From Spain to France to Germany to Australia, the traditional reformist parties have utterly failed to defend workers’ interests and ward off the far-right threat. It is vital that the militant socialist left and the broader working-class movement is rebuilt to meet these challenges. And there are important opportunities to do just that.

There is a much greater opening for Marxist, working-class politics than in previous waves of protests over the last few decades. In Spain, for example, the 2011 movement of the squares provoked by the 2008 Global Financial Crisis was posed as a citizens’ movement that was neither left nor right. There was pronounced hostility to the involvement of socialist organisations and trade unions.

This time around, the movement is much more posed as a movement of the left centred on working-class demands with the involvement of revolutionary organisations welcomed. Mass strike action by workers is rightly seen as vital for the movement going forward.

In France, it was students from the poorest working-class suburbs that initiated the rebellion and the party most associated with the rebellion is Melenchon’s left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI). 

But half-way house left reformist operations like Melenchon’s LFI or the …

author: José Soeiro, Maria Manuel Rola
title: A new cycle of struggle in Portugal
content:
At the end of last June, the left and the labour movement in Portugal secured an unlikely victory: the government’s proposed labour reform, which would have overhauled the Labour Code from top to bottom, was defeated in parliament.

Public pressure was so intense — with two general strikes, dozens of protests and a campaign that rallied the majority of public opinion against the government’s violently regressive agenda — that the far right, fearful of the electoral consequences of seeing its support for such a thoroughly unpopular proposal through to the end, changed its position and ultimately joined forces with the left to vote down the government’s labour reform package.

This struggle ushered in a new cycle of confidence for the popular movement.

The government, which holds a minority in parliament, put labour issues on hold and sought to change the subject. It ensured that the Socialist Party [PS] abstained on the draft state budget, on the one hand, and, on the other, reached an agreement with the far right on a new rental law which, in practice, virtually eliminates any rights for tenants.

A two-month delay in paying rent can lead to eviction. There is no longer a cap on deposits for renting a property. The number of months’ rent a tenant must pay in advance when signing a tenancy agreement has been increased to three. The 2% cap on rent increases has been removed.

With this proposal, the rental market — which is used by those unable to buy a home — becomes even more cut-throat, in the euro zone country where house prices have risen the most, where only 2% of housing is social housing, where the rent per square metre has doubled over the last five years, where, on average, people spend 50 per cent of their income on rent for legally registered tenancies alone (that is to say, it is even worse if we take the informal market into account), and where the poverty rate rises from around 15% to 27% when housing costs are factored in.

The rising cost of living, including fuel prices, and the approval (albeit without a final vote yet) of the tenancy law have created the conditions for a new cycle of protests.

A coalition of various groups and associations, called “Não Dá Mais” (“We Can’t Take It Anymore”), organised demonstrations against the rising cost of living in five cities, on October 10, attended by several thousand people. In Porto, which has the greatest impact in the north of the country, this demonstration coincided with two other protests — in support of Palestine and to safeguard an old market (the Bulhão), which is highly symbolic for the city — and was followed by a call, inspired by events in Spain and the wave of outrage over Maricarmen’s death, to set up a tent camp at the end of the rally, occupying the square where it had taken place.

On the first night, around 30 tents were pitched and remained in place. On the second night, there were more than 50. The camp was going to be cleared by the council at the end of the second night. The activists used social media to call for a new demonstration at the same location, with the aim of deciding, at an open-air public assembly, whether to resume the sit-in. On that same day, the Mayor declared that he would be “absolutely uncompromising” if the square were to be occupied with tents again. But not even that deterred the organisers of the camp, who set it up once more, with more people and more support.

At 3am, with no journalists left in the square, the government and the city council, acting in concert, ordered a brutal police charge against a few dozen peaceful activists who had spent the night in that square. Curiously, this was on the very same day that, 20 years ago, a movement had begun to occupy the municipal theatre located in the same square.

The mobile phone videos shocked public opinion and the city. That very same day, thousands of people flocked to the square in outrage, in a massive demonstration that also made its way to the entrance of the city hall. Not only did the movement explode, but it also began to spark reactions in other cities and a huge wave of solidarity.

Not even the attempts by the government and some commentators to stigmatise and blame the activists for having “provoked the police” had any effect.

For the past 10 days, the square has been constantly filled with thousands of people in the late afternoon and evening, with cultural events and workshops, whilst the organisers manage the day-to-day running of catering …

author: Alma Torlakovic
title: Western Sydney residents in revolt after being kept in the dark over data centre
content:
In their rush to appease big tech billionaires and open up Australia as a destination for hyperscale data centres, Labor governments at all levels have demonstrated how little respect they have for the people living in their so-called “safe seats”. This is most obvious in the diverse communities of Western Sydney, where the state government has rushed to approve a dozen of these polluting, energy-intensive monstrosities.

Labor has relied on the same blueprint for each recent approval: declare the data centre as a “state significant development”, don’t let the residents know and hope that nobody checks the website for the development proposals. They have gone as far as overselling the projects on behalf of the companies, claiming that they will create jobs for the community, downplaying the hazards involved or regurgitating the idea that these are not much different from a storage warehouse.

This strategy has backfired in Guildford in Sydney’s western suburbs, where a community campaign is brewing over the state government’s approval of a $1.1 billion hyperscale data centre right next to a sports field and homes. Residents are outraged that they've been left in the dark about the 7.2-hectare data centre that will cause 24/7 noise, raise energy bills, emit carcinogenic fumes, lower people's house prices and have a huge impact on water usage and carbon emissions. We are determined to stop it, as other communities have.

An information session organised by Cumberland City Council on 24 October to address the growing community backlash to the project turned into an angry row as 100 local residents turned on council officials, the mayor and local Labor MP, Julia Finn. Residents accused them of leaving them in the dark about the project, with most only learning of the 68-megawatt data centre plans in their neighbourhood during the past fortnight. Finn, who claimed that letters had been sent to residents, was booed down by angry constituents who said that no such thing had happened.

Robyn Hann, who is spearheading the action group to stop the data centre build, said:

“We went to the [council] information session hoping to learn more and have our concerns addressed regarding health, water, pollution, 24/7 noise, house prices and other issues. Instead, we got smoke and mirrors … I felt we were completely ignored.”

One woman summed it up, telling the meeting that she had lived in the area and worked hard for 30 years to pay off her home and build a life, only to be blindsided by this project.

Western Sydney residents are sick and tired of being taken for granted by the Labour Party and being the dumping ground for polluting industries. I have published a

petition

 to demand that the Cumberland City Council and the NSW government put an immediate stop to this project. It has already gathered over 4,000 signatures. 

Goodman Group, the company behind the proposed data centre, recently had to withdraw plans to build a data centre in Lane Cove following community opposition. Gregory Goodman, CEO of Goodman Group, has added a $20 million penthouse in Double Bay to his suite of multi-million-dollar mansions in upmarket Woollahra. He’s certainly not building a data centre next to any of his luxury properties.

Since the initial council information session, community pressure has forced the council to adopt a more moderate stance. It says that it will explore legal avenues to challenge the development. At federal level, sensing widespread hostility to mega data centres, the Albanese government has announced plans to ban them in residential areas in city suburbs. But these regulations will not apply to existing approvals. 

And we cannot leave things in the hands of the politicians and bureaucrats because the law is stacked in favour of big business. We must continue to pressure the state government and local Labor member. 

A community forum on 26 October organised by independent councillor Ahmed Ouf to oppose the project drew 200 people at Guildford Leagues Club. A similar number showed up to the council meeting on 28 October to register their opposition to the proposal.

NSW Socialists have played a central role in this campaign. We have doorknocked thousands of homes in the area, gathering signatures for the petition, talking to local residents.

The NSW government and Julia Finn could intervene to stop this project if they wanted. But they’re more interested in appeasing tech billionaires. That’s just one more reason we …

author: Ben Radford
title: UN General Assembly votes to end US blockade of Cuba — again
content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-thirty countries voted in favour of the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba” on October 28, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.

Every year since 1992, the UNGA has overwhelmingly voted to end the blockade. However, this year, there was a rise in votes against and abstentions, likely reflective of new far-right governments — for example, in Colombia, Chile and Honduras — coming to power since last year’s vote. The US has also ramped up its international efforts to isolate Cuba through sanctions and threats of sanctions against countries that trade with Cuba.

This year’s vote took place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

On top of existing strangulation mechanisms, the US government imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January, claiming that the country posed an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.

The US announced tariffs on goods from countries that, directly or indirectly, sold or provided oil to Cuba. Following the US’s January 3 attacks on Venezuela, it also blocked all Venezuelan oil shipments to the country.

The energy blockade is the reason for widespread blackouts, as well as disruptions to water supply, waste collection and transport.

The fuel shortages are severely impacting hospital operations, including treatments that require a steady energy supply, such as haemodialysis. There are harrowing reports of surgeons having to perform operations by mobile phone lights, due to the blackouts.

The US blockade has affected Cubans’ access to vital treatment and medicine. One example is Cuba’s cancer survival rates, which, while still higher than many low- and middle-income countries, have dropped from 85% to 65%.

Cuba’s infant mortality has risen from 4 out of 1000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 last year — a 148% rise.

Cuban authorities say that the current transport crisis is more acute than during the “Special Period” in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which plunged Cuba into a prolonged economic crisis. Fuel shortages have affected refrigerated transport, preventing more than 30,000 children from receiving vaccines.

In May, the US imposed a regime of secondary sanctions against governments and companies that invest in or trade with Cuba.

For example, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has imposed fines on US companies for handling cargo shipments bound for Cuba and providing services for people living in the country.

Over the past year, 34 international banking institutions suspended or declined to conduct operations with Cuba, citing risks of secondary sanctions.

Several airlines have ceased operations in Cuba and many international hotel chains also abandoned management agreements for hotels, citing the risks posed by the secondary sanctions regime. These sanctions — along with other US measures — have contributed to the collapse in Cuba’s tourism industry.

“The application of these measures has produced a sophisticated mechanism of asphyxiation directed at the Cuban population, exceeding by far the levels of pressure historically imposed over decades,” the annual report said.

It also notes that the blockade has caused US$3.9 trillion worth of damages since it was imposed. However, it said the impacts go far beyond economic losses, causing suffering, illness and death.

The US blockade of Cuba violates not just international law, but any semblance of humanity.

The US government has made its intention of achieving “regime change” in Cuba by the end of the year very clear; it is openly considering the possibility of military attacks. This has been the US’s policy since Cubans overthrew the …

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Mass protests defeat the far right in Brazil, but Lula is no way forward
content:
With the winds in Latin America blowing decisively towards the far right over recent years, voters went to the polls in the continent’s most important country, Brazil, in October. The Workers’ Party (PT), led by long-time leader and incumbent president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, lost in the first round, but achieved a remarkable turnaround in the second round.

Lula, as he is popularly known, was running against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, Lula’s predecessor. Jair is currently serving a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup after he lost the 2022 election. During his term he oversaw the deaths of over 700,000 people during the pandemic and is a close ally of President Trump. 

In the first round, Flavio Bolsonaro won 47 percent against Lula’s 45 percent. The right also took control of Congress.

The PT’s first-round loss shows how much support the PT has lost among its traditional base. The outgoing Lula administration was committed to a fiscal framework of zero budget deficits, resulting in caps on public spending and wages. It also allowed further oil exploration of the Amazon. During the campaign, Lula gave ground to the right's tough-on-crime platform, indicating his support for lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16.

The PT’s poor performance in the first round makes its turnaround in the second round even more impressive. Over the three weeks, the PT’s vote increased by over ten million, giving the party 52 percent of the vote. Facing criminal allegations of money laundering, Bolsonaro fled to Miami.

The key factor in the sharp jump in the PT vote was the huge rallies that spread across the country between the two rounds of voting. The day after the first round, students at the Federal University in Rio de Janeiro held an assembly that turned into a rally, spilling out onto the streets. Social media and WhatsApp groups exploded with calls for demonstrations. On 7 October, the National Union of Students called demonstrations in several major cities that saw tens of thousands come out. 

These initial demonstrations were about mobilising to defeat the far right, defending public education, and fighting to reduce the work week to five days from six, a demand that Lula’s government has resisted. Although backing for the PT’s re-election was present, it received much less emphasis. One slogan was: “No to the father, no to the son.”

By 9 October, even small cities were holding assemblies and demonstrations. In Ponta Grossa, a city of around 350,000, university and high school students held an assembly of over a thousand people, promoted as “students against fascism”. It decided on an action plan that included leafleting and door knocking. Similar scenes played out at universities across the country.

“The first few days after the election were like a frenzy”, said Veronica O’Kelly, a national leader of the socialist group Revolucão Socialista. She continued,

“WhatsApp groups promoted rallies across the country. Students led demonstrations out of the universities into the streets. Their demands were immediately far beyond anything the PT was offering. This is what kicked off the mass demonstrations that came over the following weeks.” 

On the first weekend after the first round over one million joined marches in Sao Paolo and Rio de Janeiro under the slogan “The class is in the streets”. Lula was a prominent feature of the rallies, standing on top of a bus in Sao Paolo, surrounded by throngs of people. In other cities, hundreds of thousands joined marches. 

But students remained the driving force. On 14 October, the student union at the University of Brasilia held a demonstration of over 50,000 in the capital under the slogan “Bolsonaro never again and end the 6x1 now,” referring to the six-day work week.

The fact that the rallies raised major economic demands alongside support for the PT put pressure on Lula not just to offer promises after the second round but to take immediate action. On 14 October, Congress passed a constitutional amendment reducing the work week from six days to five with no loss of salary. This was a monumental victory for the Brazilian working class that the movement imposed on not just the PT but the entire ruling class. The measure passed the Senate 75 to 1, with even Bolsonaro’s party voting for it.

Another notable point of the election was several strong results for the left. Several far-left organisations inside the …

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Unmasked agendas: Macron, youth protests and blocking social media
content:
Finally, the ill-fitting mask on the ugly face of government policy comes off. In the sunset of his administration, French President Emmanuel Macron is facing a boiling, indignant movement that began with the protests of disgruntled students and has burgeoned into something much more significant.

Teachers at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in the southeastern Parisian suburb of Créteil went on strike over severe staff shortages, on September 17. Students and parents added themselves to the strike. The school entrance was blocked, videos taken and social media platforms used to disseminate the message.

A blooming followed through to October, drawing in some 3700 schools and hundreds and thousands of protesters. Social, economic and political angst had been stirred, with grievances focused on inadequate provision of teaching, packed classrooms, overburdened schedules and the dilapidation of school infrastructure. The university admissions platform Parcoursup also came in for criticism.

As part of the response to the protests, Macron has, as is traditional with a smug incumbent caught off guard, identified an aggravating, foreign influence steering matters. Conveniently for him, the fault seems to lie with the progenitors of the social media world, those United States Big Tech beasts and platforms that have turned users into anything from bovine consumers to adept, resourceful users of technology. It’s the resourceful aspect of the technology that is proving particularly troubling for government officialdom.

As one of the last acts of his administration, France’s desperate leader has attempted to impose age-restrictions on users of social media platforms ostensibly as a therapeutic exercise.

In doing so, he has joined a wide tent of invigilating governments keen to use the alleged malignancies of social media as an alibi for controlling access to certain online platforms, a mood captured by the efforts of the European Union to advance the all suppressing EU Kids Act. (Australia was the first to bolt out of the stables last December with its Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024, paraded as a noble effort to limit the use of social platforms by those under 16 years of age. Unsurprisingly, it is showing itself to be a foolish legislative bauble, weak and circumvented.)

On July 21, the French parliament adopted the “Loi visant à protéger les mineurs face aux risques associés à l’usage des réseaux sociaux” (Law aiming to protect minors from the risks associated with social media usage), an alleged palliative for the ills (examples include anxiety, depression and sleep disorders) of using social media for those under 15. This exaggerated sense of moral success did not last long.

In August, France’s Constitutional Council poured cold water on the government’s grand strategy, striking down the legislation as needlessly broad and hopelessly excessive. The access to the platforms, for instance, was “not subject to any condition relating to the functionalities or content offered, the dangers they expose users, and the inadequacy of the safeguards with which they are provided.”

Saliently, the Council noted that the ban encumbered the rights of young people to access information and engage in the democratic system. This meant retarding the useful instruction of children to meaningfully engage the political process on ceasing to be minors. Social networking platforms were not inherently wicked things; they could also serve as educational tools, promote civic engagement and aid in building communities.

A chastened Macron proceeded to direct Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to make the necessary adjustments in line with the Council’s decision.

The response from Macron to these youth-inspired protests, in light of his stuttering efforts against the corruptions of social media, is a more candid reflection on why governments seek to restrict any platform that adds vim to dissent and disagreement.

In remarks made to members of law enforcement during his October 26 visit to Marseille City Hall, the president scorned social media sites for “damaging our democracies” and being “tools for mobilising the worst impulses”. They had brought “young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place.”

author: Nick Everett
title: Will Israel’s election outcome make life better for Palestinians? Not likely.
content:
In the lead-up to Israel’s 27 October election, media headlines declared this would be the most “consequential” in Israel’s history. At stake is the fate of Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who faces corruption charges at home and an international arrest warrant for war crimes in Gaza.

Israeli politicians debated the cost of living, the independence of the judiciary, conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military, a state inquiry into security failings on 7 October and Israel’s growing isolation abroad. Not up for debate was Israel’s Gaza genocide, nor the massive expansion of Israeli settlements, settler violence and military invasions in the West Bank, nor Israel’s seizure of territory in southern Lebanon and Syria. 

This was a contest between two blocs, a pro-Netanyahu coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties against an alliance of centrist and right-wing Zionist parties seeking to depose him, led by retired General Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff. A third bloc, made up of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, was initially barred from participation by Israel’s Central Elections Committee before the supreme court overturned the ban.

Right-wing parties Likud and Otzma Yehudit petitioned for their exclusion, accusing the Arab-majority parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism. A ban was, however, upheld against Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party and one of the Joint List candidates, on the grounds that he had supported armed struggle against Israel. 

The evidence? An opinion piece published in 

Alaraby

 on 8 October 2023, in which Abu Shehadeh described the previous day’s Hamas-led attack on Israel as a “significant historical event”. 

Accusations of “inciting racism” against Ra’am and the Arab List are of course rank hypocrisy coming from Netanyahu and his coalition partners who have 

called for

 the “total annihilation” of Gaza’s cities and the burning of Lebanon, as well as the death penalty for Palestinians accused of “terrorism” offences.

On the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s social media posts drew attention to long queues of Palestinian voters at polling stations and urged Likud supporters to come out and vote.

“If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi”, he said, referring to the leaders of the two Arab-majority parties.

Netanyahu’s coalition ally and Jewish supremacist Itamar Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout—people exercising their democratic right to vote—as “crazy”. As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has armed Israeli settlers and established a paramilitary police force in the West Bank.

Basel Smotrich, another Jewish supremacist Netanyahu ally, and leader of the Religious Zionism party, announced he had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what he described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters, alleging voter fraud. 

While Netanyahu failed to win this election, he remains far from defeated. His ruling coalition, dominated by Likud, will likely secure 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, a major drop from the 64 seats he won in 2022, and significantly short of a majority. However, the opposition bloc is trailing with 48 seats. The opposition’s only pathway to power is to govern with the support of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, which together secured an additional 19 seats (nearly double the ten they secured in 2022).

This would not be unprecedented. In 1993, the Oslo Accords were signed by a minority Israeli government with the support of the Arab List parties.

In 2021, Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas broke with the Arab List to join an eight-party coalition, the first time an Arab-majority party had joined an Israeli government. For Abbas, this was an opportunity to secure some short-lived investment in Palestinian communities inside Israel, while turning his back on the elephant in the room: the Israeli occupation. The coalition collapsed within a year following defections from its right flank.

Abbas has declared his intention again to seek a coalition that can unseat Netanyahu. His Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on its slate. However, such overtures have so far been rebuffed.  …

author: Mat Ward
title: 10 new underrated protest albums that should be topping the charts
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for October.

New South Wales' Labor government backed Queensland's ban on Palestine freedom slogans on October 1. The move came as Jewish US protest singer David Rovics released probably his catchiest album yet, containing songs "all about the US-Israeli Epstein Empire", before touring Australia. On album opener "The Holocaust Is Now", featuring backing vocals from Green Left writer Kamala Emanuel, he sings: "Can you spend two hundred dollars to buy a loaf of bread? Neither can the Palestinians, they’re dying instead." The LP was released while donkey prices in Gaza surged from $US1000 to $US30,000 "due to the virtual elimination of motorised private transport". As Israel's election loomed on October 28, the album's title track, "Rise", called for Israelis to rise up against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was being endorsed by US President Donald Trump as a "great warrior" who must be re-elected so they could "finish the job" in their disastrous war on Iran. "Overthrow your theocratic state, before it is too late," sings Rovics. "Reject your leaders and their lies. Rise, Israelis, rise!" LISTEN>>>

One of the seemingly few Israelis rising up is pop-rock musician Regev Baruch, with his scathing new album, Super Sparta. Its title is a phrase coined by Netanyahu last year to describe his commitment to eternal war. Discussing the LP, which likens Israelis to Nazis, Baruch said: “There’s this graffiti that says, ‘Grandma, what were you doing during the genocide?’ I was looking for a good answer to that — something I could do to prove I wasn’t part of the silent majority... In the end, I said, ‘OK, there are journalists; they’re investigating. There are lawyers; they’re fighting a legal battle. You’re a musician — just make music.’ That’s the most powerful thing I can do.” Of course, Baruch is far from the only Jewish person publicly condemning Israel's genocide against Palestinians, as shown by the countless Jews who attended vigils marking three years of the war on October 7. Meanwhile, pro-Palestine punks Amyl and the Sniffers, whose new live LP blasts fascistic leaders, said they were donating proceeds from an upcoming Bondi gig to "extend our love" to Jews affected by the Bondi attack. LISTEN>>>

English feminist rage musician Delilah Bon, who paints her body with slogans such as "Free Palestine", also released a new live album on October 16 as her Australian tour loomed. The LP documents a show she played to reach out to American fans after she had to cancel a US tour due to fears about the country's Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. The event, which raised £8,000 for organisations supporting people affected by ICE, opens with the apt "Illegal Aliens" and powers through fan favourites such as "Dead Men Don't Rape", "War On Women" and "Princeless Princess". On the excoriating "Not The President", she sings: "That's not the president, that's just some man, who has abused so many women and children... There's so much love in this world, I'm holding hands with every girl that cries alone in her room, that fears this world is so fucking doomed." She then gets her British fans to chant "fuck Trump" for their peers in the US. The explosive power of her dayglo-daubed live show, in which she goes from pitch-perfect singing to razor-sharp rapping and searing screaming, is inspiring. LISTEN>>>

Also condemning ICE is the new LP from Grammy-winning folk musician Mary Gauthier, released days before an agent in New York shot into a car with a child inside. On "Soldier Of Fortune" she cites ICE victims Renée Good and Alex Pretti as she sings: "You're nothing but a gun for hire, hiding behind a mask. You didn't care if she was somebody's mother, when you shot her in the face through the window glass. A VA nurse on a city street, full of the courage you lack. An angel of mercy, helping a stranger and you fired 10 bullets into his back." That preceded the October 16 LP from Heavens To Betsy, the kind of riot grrrl pioneers who paved the way for the likes of Delilah Bon. The LP, a long-lost 1992 demo released to mark their reformation, centres on "My Secret" in which singer Corin Tucker blasts an abuser. author: Unknown
title: VOLVAC patronu adını gizleyerek işçi arıyor
content:
Barış Salık [email protected] Murat Uysal [email protected]

İstanbul – Tuzla’daki VOLVAC Paketleme ve Gıda Makinaları Fabrikasının önünde kurulan çadırda direniş 8. gününe girdi. DİSK/Birleşik Metal-İş’e üye oldukları için işten çıkarılan 35 işçi fabrika kapısında bekliyor. Bu işçiler, üretimde çalışanların tamamı. Fabrikada üretim yok. İşçilerin anlattığına göre şirket yeni işçi aramak için ilan açtı. İlanlarda fabrikanın adresi birebir yer alıyor ama şirketin adı geçmiyor. İşçilerin aktardığına göre fabrikanın önünde ilk günden bu yana yaklaşık 100 polis bekliyor.

İşçi Yıldıray örgütlenme fikrinin nasıl olgunlaştığını şöyle anlattı: “Bir iş arkadaşımız vardı, işini de iyi yapan biriydi. Sebepsiz yere 25/2 ile işten atıldı. Biz zaten bir süredir içeride koşulların kötüleştiğini konuşuyorduk. Bir gün toplu bir şekilde cuma namazına giderken cami yolunda ‘Sendikaya üye olalım’ diye bir fikir geliştirdik. Ardından hızla örgütlenmeye başladık. İçeride birkaç kişi hariç herkes örgütlendi.”

İş Kanunu’nun 25/II maddesi, işverene “Ahlak ve iyi niyet kurallarına uymayan haller” gerekçesiyle işçiyi bildirimsiz ve tazminatsız çıkarma imkanı veriyor.

Eylül ayında örgütlenmesini tamamlayan işçiler yetki başvurusu yaptı. Çalışma ve Sosyal Güvenlik Bakanlığının yetki tespit yazısı 15 Ekim’de geldi. Yıldıray, sonrasında yaşananları şöyle aktardı: “Yetkinin ardından patron Birleşik Metal-İş genel başkanıyla görüştü. Görüşme olumlu geçse de daha sonra çalıştığı avukatı değiştirdi. Hemen ardından da birimlerinde şef ve sorumlu olan, ben dahil 5 arkadaşı işten attı.” Atılan 5 işçi 26 Ekim Pazartesi sabahı fabrika kapısının önünde direnişe başladı. İçeride çalışmaya devam eden işçiler de arkadaşlarına sahip çıktı. Yıldıray şöyle anlattı: “Bu işten atmayla beraber çalışmaya devam eden arkadaşlarımız içeride eylemler yaptı. Biz kapı önüne çadır kurmuştuk, aralarda gelip bize destek oldular, sloganlar attılar. Geçtiğimiz cuma günü de içerideki 30 arkadaşımızı işten attılar. Şimdi 35 kişi burada mücadelemizi sürdürüyoruz.”

Yıldıray, işten atmalar karşısında devletin tutumunu da sorguluyor: “Burada içimizden biri bıçaklansa, bir saldırıya uğrasa polis gelmeyecek. Mesele patronun güvenliği olduğunda burada birikiyor. Bu kolluk kimi koruyor şimdi? İlk günden beri 100 polis bizim başımızı bekliyor, daha doğrusu patronun malını bekliyor. Oysa biz anayasal hakkımızı kullandık. Madde ne diyor? İşçi istediği sendikaya üye olabilir diyor. Eğer öyleyse patron bizi işten atarak suç işliyor, kanuna karşı geliyor. Ama bu kanunu koruyan kanunların da olması lazım. İşçiler işten atılırken patrona ‘Bunları niye işten atıyorsun?’ diye soracak devlet lazım.”

Anayasa’nın 51. maddesi, çalışanlara önceden izin almaksızın sendikalara üye olma hakkı tanıyor. 6356 sayılı Sendikalar ve Toplu İş Sözleşmesi Kanunu da sendika üyeliği nedeniyle işten çıkarmayı yasaklıyor. Birleşik Metal-İş İstanbul 1 No’lu Şube Başkanı Can Emrah Ülgü de geçen hafta patronlara danışmanlık yapan avukatlık bürolarına dikkat çekmişti. Ülgü’ye göre bu bürolar süreci sendikasızlaştırma üzerine kuruyor ve patronlara yol haritası sunuyor.

VOLVAC, gıda paketleme makineleri üretiyor ve ağırlıklı olarak ihracata çalışıyor. Şirket, tanıtımında ABD, Rusya, Çin ve Almanya dahil 42’den fazla ülkeye satış yaptığını söylüyor. Sendikaya göre siparişler yoğun. Ancak üretimde çalışan işçilerin tamamı atıldığı için fabrikada üretim durmuş durumda. İçeride yalnızca sekreterlik, insan kaynakları ve satış bölümlerinde çalışanlar kaldı.

İşçiler, daha bir hafta öncesine kadar siparişler yetişsin diye enselerinde boza pişiren patronun şimdi ne yaptığını merak ediyor.

Sorunun yanıtına dair bir ipucu bir iş ilanından geldi. İşçilerin anlattığına göre şirket yeni işçi arıyor. İlanda fabrikanın adresi birebir yer alıyor ama şirketin adı geçmiyor.

author: Sophia Sheera
title: Labour Ends Power-Sharing With Green Councils Over ‘Zionism Is Racism’ Policy
content:
Labour has pulled out of power-sharing coalitions with the Green party in 11 councils after party members voted to adopt a policy designating Zionism as a form of racism.


Green party members voted to adopt the policy at the party’s annual conference on 4 October. Prime minister Andy Burnham

denounced the policy

days later, labelling it “antisemitic” and declaring that his party would “have nothing to do with it”. 


Labour councillors will no longer work with their Green colleagues in local authorities including Sheffield, Warwick, West Devon and Lewes, potentially disrupting local services for hundreds of thousands of people. 


“Labour are trying to bully everyone into defending Genocide,”

wrote Green party leader Zack Polanski on X

. “We will not cower. We will not be bullied from speaking the truth.”


Agreements remain in six councils, where Green groups have met Labour’s conditions. On 16 October, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said

local groups would have to publicly reject

 the ‘Zionism Is Racism’ policy and ask Polanski to reconsider it. 


The Greens said that by intervening, Labour has “forced local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents”. 


They added that Labour has “failed to respect the choices made by local voters” and “ignored the judgements of their own local leaders”.


The move from Labour comes despite Burnham’s promises of greater control for local authorities as part of his plans to devolve power away from Westminster. 


The Green party operates under direct democracy, with policies decided by members. The Zionism motion won more than 1,000 votes despite facing criticism from four of the party’s five MPs.

author: David Swanson
title: Canada’s Largest Labor Federation Votes to Block Arms Shipments Bound for Israel
content:
By

The Cradle

, November 2, 2026


In a statement published on October 28, the Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents some 3 million workers, called on its members to block the handling of all weapons and military equipment passing through Canada to Israel.


“The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC) Canadian Council has voted in support of a resolution calling on workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel,” the 

statement

 reads.


The CLC added that it “stands in solidarity with Palestinian workers and their families, and with all those calling for peace, justice and respect for international law.”


The federation said Canada bears responsibility for ensuring that arms manufactured on its soil are not used against Palestinian civilians or in violation of international humanitarian law, and urged the government in Ottawa to halt all direct and indirect transfers of weapons and military equipment to Israel.


The CLC called on Ottawa to uphold international law, protect civilian lives and back a just and lasting peace for Palestinians and Israelis.


Despite Canada claiming to have restricted or paused arms transfers to Israel, shipping and import records point to a 

continuous flow

 of weapons and military components.


A 

July 2025 report

, ‘Exposing Canadian Military Exports to Israel,’ compiled by the Palestinian Youth Movement, World Beyond War, and the Arms Embargo Now Campaign, found that a continuous, multi-million-dollar pipeline of military supplies, ammunition, and components flowed directly from Canada to Israel.


Analyzing commercial shipping records and Israel Tax Authority import data from October 2023 to July 2025, the groups uncovered 47 direct commercial shipments from Canadian arms manufacturers and 391 military-relevant import records.


The transfers took place under previously approved export permits, by sea and on more than 100 flights. Of those, 64 were commercial passenger flights carrying military cargo in the hold beneath civilian travelers.


The vast majority went to 

Elbit Systems

, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, and its subsidiaries.


Some shipments were even accelerated, according to the groups, with cargo at times rerouted through third countries such as the US to reach Israel.


Months after Ottawa announced its ban in March 2024, reports emerged that $60 million worth of munitions from a $20 billion arms sale to Israel approved by Washington were set to be manufactured in Canada.


The CLC’s demand comes amid a wave of coordinated dockworker

strikes

 across five continents.


According to Italy’s Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), more than 25 unions moved on Friday to prevent arms shipments bound for war zones from passing through 113 civilian ports in 22 countries and regions.


Rallying under a 

joint declaration

 adopted in Istanbul in May, the unions demanded an immediate end to Israel’s genocide of the Palestinians in Gaza and international recognition of an independent Palestinian state on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, and refused to allow any port to serve as a channel for weapons, ammunition, or troops bound for war zones.

World BEYOND War
