author: Sophie Lemcke
title: So ist es, als weibliches Rind in der Milchindustrie zu leben
content:
Die Milchindustrie ist ein grausamer Kreislauf des Leids und endet mit einem gewaltvollen Tod.


Wie fühlt es sich an, in dieses System hineingeboren zu werden, ohne die Möglichkeit, dem zu entkommen?


Der einzige Grund, weshalb die Industrie dich „produziert“ hat: Auch du sollst Kinder gebären, immer wieder, damit du Milch produzierst. Milch, die dann von Menschen, statt von deinem Kalb konsumiert werden kann.


Du wirst fixiert, während jemand das Besamungsgerät in deine Vagina sowie seinen Arm in deinen Anus einführt. Wenn die Zwangsbefruchtung nicht beim ersten Mal zur Trächtigkeit führt – was oft der Fall ist –, wird dieser Vorgang mehrfach wiederholt.


Neun Monate – wie bei uns Menschen – wächst dein Kalb in dir heran. Du spürst eine Verbindung, merkst, wie es sich bewegt und immer größer wird. Je schwerer du selbst wirst, umso stärker werden deine Gelenkprobleme. Die rutschigen und harten Spaltenböden, auf denen du fast dein ganzes Leben verbringst, führen oft zu Verletzungen.


Dann bringst du dein Kalb zur Welt. Um dich herum riecht es extrem nach Kot und Ammoniak, von den Ausscheidungen der Tiere.


Endlich ist es da, noch ganz nass und schwach. Du leckst ihm über das Fell, um es zu wärmen. Es sucht deine Nähe und will an deinem Euter die für ihn so wichtige Erstmilch trinken. Sie stärkt sein noch schwaches Immunsystem und gibt ihm Kraft. Doch dann kommen die Arbeiter*innen.


Sie zerren dein noch ganz wackelig stehendes Kalb weg von dir. Es ruft nach dir. Du versuchst, bei ihm zu bleiben, aber du hast keine Chance. Die Menschen haben es weggebracht – du wirst es wahrscheinlich nie wiedersehen und nach nur zwei Monaten direkt wieder gewaltvoll befruchtet.


Du wirst nach der Geburt monatelang mehrmals täglich in den Melkstand getrieben – und die meiste Zeit davon bist du bereits wieder schwanger. Dein Körper muss gleichzeitig ein neues Kalb versorgen, das in dir heranwächst, und täglich über 22 Liter Milch produzieren. Dein Euter und deine Zitzen schmerzen. Aufgrund der extremen Überzüchtung produzierst du viermal so viel Milch, wie du es natürlicherweise für dein Kind tun würdest.


Die Prozeduren und Haltungsbedingungen zehren stark an deinem Körper. Dein Euter ist entzündet und schmerzt bei jeder Berührung. Andere Tiere humpeln, weil ihnen jeder Schritt wehtut. Viele sind schwach und ausgelaugt.


Wenn du nicht schon vorher stirbst oder getötet wirst, weil dein Körper nicht mehr kann, dann wirst du voraussichtlich nach nur fünf Jahren getötet – obwohl du unter natürlichen Bedingungen 25 Jahre alt werden könntest.


Dann kommt der Tag, an dem du als nicht mehr profitabel giltst. Du wirst aus dem Stall getrieben – das erste Mal nach Jahren verlässt du ihn, aber das ist kein Grund zur Freude.


Zusammen mit anderen erschöpften „ausgedienten Milchkühen“ wirst du auf einen Transporter verladen. Du hast Mühe, über die Rampe zu gehen. Deine Gelenke schmerzen vom jahrelangen Stehen auf Spaltenböden. Im engen Transporter stehst du dicht an dicht mit den anderen Tieren, der Lkw wackelt. Manche fallen hin und werden versehentlich getreten. Eure Fahrt in den Schlachthof dauert mehrere Stunden, ohne Wasser, ohne Nahrung, ohne Pause.


Angekommen erwartet dich ein brutaler Tod. Überall riecht es nach Blut, du bekommst Panik, aber es gibt keinen Ausweg. Dann ein Bolzenschuss in deinen Kopf. Wenn die Betäubung korrekt durchgeführt wurde und wirkt, brichst du zusammen. Wenn nicht, kann es sein, dass du bei Bewusstsein und unter extremen Schmerzen erlebst, wie dir deine Kehle aufgeschnitten wird und du verblutest.


Es ist unvorstellbar, was Mutterrinder in der Milchindustrie erleiden müssen.


Der wahre Preis von Milch


Ein Ermittler von Animal Equality hat mehrere Monate undercover in einem deutschen Milchgewinnungsbetrieb gearbeitet und den Alltag der Tiere dokumentiert. Was unsere Undercover-Recherche zeigt, ist der wahre Preis von Milch: Ausbeutung, Gewalt, Schmerz, Leid und Tod.


Auf unserer Webseite erfährst du mehr und kannst die Stellungnahme des Betriebs nachlesen:


Zur Undercover-Recherche


Unterstütze dieses grausame System nicht!


Entscheide dich konsequent für pflanzliche Lebensmittel. Im Supermarkt findest du zahlreiche Alternativen zu Milch, wie:


Hafermilch – mild, cremig, perfekt für Kaffee und Müsli (oft die günstigste Option!)


Sojamilch – proteinreich, ideal zum Kochen und Backen


Mandelmilch – leicht nussig, besonders lecker in Smoothies


Reismilch – süßlich und gut verträglich …

author: L214
title: Enquête abattoir Cooperl
content:
L214 publie une enquête sur l’étourdissement des cochons au CO₂ dans l’un des plus gros abattoirs de France : l’abattoir Cooperl de Montfort-sur-Meu, en Ille-et-Vilaine (Bretagne).

Les images, commentées par l'écrivaine Marie Darrieussecq, montrent la cruauté de cette méthode d'étourdissement dont les instances scientifiques ont établi qu’elle est source de peur, de détresse et de souffrance.

Plus de trente vétérinaires signent un appel publié ce jour pour demander l’interdiction du gazage au CO₂ des cochons. L214 se joint à cette demande et entame un recours contre l’État pour faire interdire cette pratique. L’enseigne de supermarchés Carrefour fait fabriquer par son partenaire Cooperl ses produits à base de viande de porc sous ses marques distributeurs, notamment sa marque Filière Qualité Carrefour. L’association demande à Carrefour de refuser le gazage des cochons et de signer le Plant Protein Pact.

Le musicien Moby apporte son soutien et appelle à signer la pétition.

Chaque heure d’abattage, plus de 800 cochons sont gazés au CO₂ à l’abattoir Cooperl de Montfort-sur-Meu, en Bretagne. Plongés dans une fosse à haute concentration en CO₂, les cochons ont la sensation de se noyer : ils hurlent, paniquent, cherchent désespérément à fuir. Il leur faut entre 21 et 60 secondes pour perdre conscience…

Ce n’est ni instantané, ni sans souffrance. Les instances scientifiques européenne (EFSA) et britannique (AWC) l’affirment depuis 20 ans : cette méthode provoque douleur, peur et détresse respiratoire. Le Royaume-Uni envisage même d’y renoncer, et plus de trente vétérinaires demandent son interdiction.

Pourtant, l’abattoir Cooperl de Montfort-sur-Meu a investi en 2024 environ 5 millions d'euros dans cet équipement qui permet d’abattre un nombre gigantesque d’animaux, de conquérir de nouveaux marchés, d’augmenter les cadences et la productivité. L’enseigne Carrefour fait fabriquer par son partenaire Cooperl des produits à base de cochons gazés sous ses marques, dont la Filière Qualité Carrefour, tout en se disant « pionnier sur le bien-être animal »…

À l’État français : interdire le gazage au CO₂ des cochons ;

À Carrefour : ne plus s’approvisionner en produits issus de cochons gazés et participer à un changement collectif en s'engageant dans le Plant Protein Pact, pour prendre part à une réduction de moitié du nombre d’animaux tués d’ici 2030.

Plus nous serons nombreux et nombreuses, plus il sera difficile pour les responsables de fermer les yeux. Signez et partagez : les cochons ne peuvent pas parler pour eux-mêmes, mais nous, oui.

author: PETA-Team
title: Ukraine: Freiwilliger Tierretter und Hund sterben nach Drohnenangriff
content:
Am 27. Oktober 2026 wurde ein Team von PETAs Partnerorganisation

Animal Rescue Kharkiv

 bei einer

Tierrettung in der Ukraine

 angegriffen: Zwei Drohnen trafen das Fahrzeug der Helfer:innen, zerschlugen die Windschutzscheibe und verletzten den 40-jährigen Helfer Jesse Adams und einen der geretteten Hunde tödlich. Wir von PETA Deutschland und unsere internationalen Partnerorganisationen betrauern den Verlust des engagierten Freiwilligen aus Kanada. 


Gleichzeitig zeigt der tödliche Angriff auf unser Partnerteam, wie gefährlich die Lage im ukrainischen Kriegsgebiet weiterhin für alle Lebewesen ist. Erfahren Sie hier mehr zu dem Angriff und wie Sie unseren Partnern und den Tieren vor Ort helfen können.

 

 


Schwerer Angriff auf Tierrettungsteam: Russische Drohnen töten Helfer bei der Rettung von Tieren und setzen Unterkunft in Brand 


Der tödliche Angriff ereignete sich, als Jesse Adams aus dem kanadischen Vancouver Island, und andere zivile Retter:innen unserer Partnerorganisation

Animal Rescue Kharkiv

 (ARK) Tiere in einen Transporter luden – einige von ihnen verletzt, alle vom Krieg tief verängstigt und evakuierungsbedürftig.  


Zwei Drohnen trafen das Fahrzeug, zerschlugen die Windschutzscheibe, verletzten Adams mit einer massiven Splitterexplosion und töteten einen

der geretteten Hunde

. Eine weitere Drohne traf das Haus, in dem die Tiere kurzfristig bis zur Abholung in das Projekt von ARK untergebracht waren, und setzte es in Brand.  


Rettungskräfte eilten herbei, um das Feuer zu löschen, Adams wurde sofort ins Krankenhaus transportiert – doch er verstarb während der Notoperation aufgrund seiner schweren Verletzungen. 


Weiterer Angriff auf vorübergehende Unterkunft der geretteten Tiere 


Währenddessen schlugen erneut zwei weitere Drohnen in das Haus ein, in dem die Tiere kurzfristig untergebracht waren. Die Unterkunft brannte lichterloh – doch alle Tiere konnten in Sicherheit gebracht werden. Dennoch sind alle Beteiligten schwer traumatisiert – das Einsatzteam und die

geretteten Tiere

. 


„Tiere führen keine Kriege, aber sie sind Opfer davon, müssen ohne Nahrung, Wasser oder tierärztliche Versorgung unter schweren Verletzungen leiden, es sei denn, jemand kommt ihnen zu Hilfe. PETA fordert alle auf, an die Tiere zu denken, die von Konflikten betroffen sind, und an die Helden, die ihr eigenes Leben riskieren, um ihnen zu helfen.“  

Ingrid Newkirk, PETA-Gründerin

 


PETA und ARK sind in tiefer Trauer um Jesse Adams  


Adams war Mitbegründer der

RainCoast Dog Rescue Society

 in Kanada und einer von zahlreichen Freiwilligen mit militärischer Grundausbildung und viel Erfahrung in gefährlichen Einsatzgebieten, die ARK-Teams vor Ort unterstützen.  


In einem seiner letzten Instagram-Beiträge vor einigen Tagen schrieb Adams darüber, wie er einer Familie geholfen hatte: Diese hatte sich geweigert, ihr Zuhause in einem Gebiet zu verlassen, das täglich von Drohnen, Bomben und Raketen getroffen wurde, bis sie wussten, dass ihre Tiere sicher evakuiert werden konnten. Adams und das ARK-Team halfen der Familie bei der Evakuierung ihrer mehr als ein Dutzend Tiere und schrieben dann über den Einsatz: 


„Wir sind die großen Risiken eingegangen, weil diese Menschen und Tiere dringend unsere Hilfe brauchten. Wir sind das Risiko eingegangen, weil wir wollten, dass jemand dasselbe für uns tut, wenn wir Hilfe brauchen. Wir sind das Risiko eingegangen, weil es nicht viele gibt, die es getan hätten.“ 


Lebensgefahr für Menschen und Tiere: Angriff zeigt erneut, wie wichtig die Hilfe vor Ort ist 


Seit Beginn des russischen Angriffskrieges im Februar 2022 unterstützen wir von PETA Deutschland gemeinsam mit unseren internationalen Partnerorganisationen durch unseren Global Compassion Fund die lebensrettende, aber auch lebensgefährliche Arbeit des ARK-Teams in der Ukraine. Denn die Retter:innen arbeiten unter der ständigen

Gefahr von Bomben

, Beschuss und Gewalt, um verängstigte, traumatisierte,

verletzte

 und oft stark unterernährte Tiere in der Ukraine zu retten.  


In den vergangenen Jahren wurde ein großes Projekt vor Ort aufgebaut, sodass bisher fast 40.000 Katzen, Hunde, Pferde und andere Tiere gerettet, medizinisch versorgt und liebevoll aufgepäppelt werden konnten.  


Immer wieder lebensgefährliche und tödliche Angriffe auf Helfer:innen

+


Adams‘ Tod ist die jüngste Tragödie, die Tierretter:innen getroffen hat, die mit PETA Deutschland und anderen Tierrettungsgruppen zusammenarbeiteten. Im Juni …

author: hsa_oryx
title: QUORN HUNT TRAINING HOUNDS TO KILL: WRITE TO YOUR MP
content:
The Hunt Saboteurs Association is asking our supporters to contact their MPs following the release of horrific drone footage involving the Quorn Hunt in Leicestershire.


Members of the Quorn Hunt use the fox’s body to encourage hounds to tear it apart.

Image: Northants Hunt Saboteurs


On Friday 16 October 2026, Northants Hunt Saboteurs filmed an incident near Kirby Bellars in which a fox was killed by hounds during a Quorn Hunt cubbing meet.


Hounds converge on the fox as hunt staff look on. Image:

Northants Hunt Saboteurs


The footage shows hounds seizing and tearing at the fox while hunt staff intervene to repeatedly encourage the hounds to attack. A hunting horn can be seen being blown over the hounds to reinforce the association between the horn call and the kill!


Take action: Contact your MP


Don’t let this disturbing footage go unnoticed.


Write to your MP, ask them to watch the video and to support robust legislation to strengthen the Hunting Act. 


Template letter below:


Organised Hunts hunting as usual – Famous Quorn Hunt filmed killing a fox


Dear [MP]


The 1st November will see the official start of the foxhunting season, but hunts have been out since August training their hounds to hunt and kill. This is called autumn hunting by them and cub hunting by the rest of us. 


This is illustrated by the film we obtained taken from a drone showing the Quorn Hunt killing a fox. This is ‘trail hunting’ in its bloody reality, and it happened just a few days ago, on the eve of the BHSA’s National Trail Hunting Day.


The full video can be viewed here:

https://www.huntsabs.org.uk/smokescreen-saturday-exposed/


Cub hunting is not some isolated activity. It is the preparation for the hunting season ahead. Throughout the autumn, young hounds are taught what to chase, what to kill and how to respond to the huntsman’s commands. What they learn – or fail to learn – during these crucial weeks sets the tone for the entire season.


This is what makes the Quorn Hunt footage so damning. It shows hounds being deliberately encouraged to seize and tear at a fox, with hunt staff repeatedly intervening to reinforce that behaviour.


As the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) and the Countryside Alliance prepared to showcase so-called ‘trail hunting’ on National Trail Hunting Day – aka Smokescreen Saturday – the Quorn Hunt provided a horrifying glimpse of the reality behind the myth of trail laying.


The BHSA and defenders of so-called trail hunting want the public to believe the same hounds will spend the season following scent trails. Yet here they are, being trained on foxes, and of course, killing to the delight of the hunters.


The footage strikes at the very heart of the trail hunting smokescreen.


We need parliament to finish the consultation and push through a real hunting ban in the next parliament term as promised in the manifesto.


Regards


[Name]


[Address]


Find contact details for your MP here

QUORN HUNT TRAINING HOUNDS TO KILL: WRITE TO YOUR MP

 appeared first on

Hunt Saboteurs Association

.

author: Unknown
title: Geothermal project in Varto: Court examines potential environmental damage
content:
A court-ordered site inspection has taken place as part of a legal dispute over a planned geothermal project on the border between the Kurdish provinces of Bingöl and Muş. A panel of experts appointed by the Bingöl Administrative Court examined the proposed drilling sites in the villages of Licik, Çermî, and Şorik in the Karlıova district. Local residents fear that the project will severely threaten their livelihoods and are demanding its cancellation.


The project, undertaken by the US-based company IGNIS H2 Energy, covers an area between Karlıova and Varto. Affected residents filed a lawsuit against the project in April. In July, the court ordered an expert assessment and an on-site inspection.


Concerns over water sources and agriculture


Numerous local residents participated in the inspection on Monday. The expert panel was accompanied by DEM Party MPs Ibrahim Akın and Sümeyye Boz, lawyers from the Diyarbakır Bar Association, and representatives of various environmental organizations from Kurdistan and Turkey.


Akın, who also serves as co-spokesperson for the DEM Party’s Ecology Commission, highlighted the local population’s ongoing resistance. He stated that the inspections would extend from Bingöl to the Varto region.


“We hope that the expert report will help protect the existing livelihoods of our people. Regardless of the report’s findings, we will stand alongside those resisting the project,” Akın said.


DEM Party MP Sümeyye Boz emphasized that the planned activities would not be limited to individual drilling sites. Rather, she said, the project would affect an extensive area encompassing numerous villages, agricultural lands, and pastures.


“This is a project stretching from Karlıova to Varto that threatens to destroy a vast area where people live and work. That is why people in both regions have been resisting it for months,” Boz said.


“Courts must decide in favor of people’s lives”


Boz stressed that the site inspection must determine, in particular, the potential impact of the planned drilling operations on settlements, water resources, agriculture, and livestock farming. She expressed hope that the expert panel would take the potential consequences into account through its direct observations on the ground.


“We hope that the courts will rule in favor of people’s lives rather than the interests of companies. We will continue our struggle,” the MP stated.


Following the completion of the inspections in Karlıova and Varto, the expert report will serve as a basis for further judicial review of the controversial geothermal project.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Microplastics in lakes near Iqaluit likely come from local source: Study
content:
Microplastics that are present in lakes around Iqaluit likely come from a local source, according to findings from a recent study published in the journal Arctic Science.


Researchers sampled 19 lakes in 2022 and 2023, including nine east of Iqaluit and 10 north of the city. The highest concentration of particles was found in lakes east — or downwind — of Iqaluit.


Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic that have broken off from larger items, such as left-behind litter. They are known to be harmful to ecosystems and human health.


The direction the wind blows is important to take into consideration because microplastics can travel long distances by air, said Patricia Corcoran, a Western University professor in the earth sciences department, and one of authors of the study, “Microplastics in stair-step moss and lake water on Baffin Island, Nunavut, reflect a local source component.”


“Wherever we go, we’re shedding microplastics,” Corcoran said in an interview, speaking from London, Ont.


Microplastics can also make their way into lakes through tributaries, creeks and rivers. Human activity, such as boating and fishing, is also a factor, she said.


Researchers found the microplastics after collecting samples of moss, lake water and shoreline sediment. They discovered the particles were mainly concentrated in moss and lake water.


Kelly Evans, the study’s lead author, visited Iqaluit two summers in a row to collect the samples, said Corcoran.


Most of what was found were microplastic fibres, Corcoran said, which are derived from textiles. Textiles that shed microplastic fibres tend to include things like rugs, nylon-based materials, or clothing.


Those contaminants get consumed by local fish and can be passed up the food chain to humans.


“There are well over 2,000 different chemicals in different plastics that are very dangerous for human health,” she said, such as known endocrine disruptors and carcinogens.


“I think it’s important that people are aware — that all communities are aware — especially remote communities who actually eat the fish on their land.”


Microplastics are known to be harmful to fish who ingest them, with prior studies finding they can cause impaired functioning, organ failure and death due to gastrointestinal blockage.


They have also been found in the stomachs and gastrointestinal tracts of freshwater fish in the Arctic, Corcoran said.


That was discovered through another study that she and Evans published in February in the journal Science of the Total Environment, which relied on fish samples from across Nunavut, the Yukon and Northwest Territories.


A total of 435 fish across seven different species were collected between 2018 and 2021 in partnership with local fishers and fisheries, with researchers finding the majority — 68 per cent — had consumed microplastics.


Fish in Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories were found to have the highest concentration of microplastics, with those found in lakes on Cornwallis Island, in the Qikiqtaaluk Region, had the second-highest concentration.


“That was a real surprise because Cornwallis Island, where Resolute is, is so far north and so remote,” Corcoran said.


Within Cornwallis Island, they found the most microplastic fragments in fish caught in Resolute Lake, near Resolute Bay. She said debris from a nearby landfill or the community’s airport may be to blame.

author: winter oak
title: Raising ourselves from the lowness of modernity
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


Ernst Friedrich Schumacher (1911-1977)

 is best remembered for his 1973 book

Small is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered

 and its message that “infinite growth in a finite environment is an obvious impossibility”. [1]


As the title of the book conveys, he saw it as important to restore a human scale to human self-organisation: “Centralisation is mainly an idea of order; decentralisation, one of freedom”. [2]


Schumacher’s attack on centralisation and economic growth went hand in hand with a broader assault on industrial society itself.


He noted in

Small is Beautiful

 that “modern man has built a system of production that ravishes nature and a type of society that mutilates man”. [3]


As I explain in my

profile

 of Schumacher on the organic radicals site, [4] he also challenged the

ways of thinking

 which have allowed the industrial

mega-racket

 [5] to gain its stranglehold on our lives.


One of these is the obsession with the idea of paid “work” – of any kind, no matter how pointless or harmful – as being an essential bulwark of everyone’s existence.


He explained: “That soul-destroying, meaningless, mechanical, monotonous, moronic work is an insult to human nature which must necessarily and inevitably produce either escapism or aggression, and that no amount of ‘bread and circuses’ can compensate for the damage done – these are facts which are neither denied nor acknowledged but are met with an unbreakable conspiracy of silence – because to deny them would be too obviously absurd and to acknowledge them would condemn the central preoccupation of modern society as a crime against humanity”. [6]


Our separation from nature is, of course, another key problem: “Modern man does not experience himself as a part of nature but as an outside force destined to dominate and destroy it”. [7]


As well as being inspired by the decentralist, degrowth economic ideas of organic radical inspirations

Mohandas Gandhi

 [8] and

Leopold Kohr

, [9] Schumacher was also influenced by the metaphysical critique of modernity voiced by the perennialist wing of the revived tradition.


In

Small is Beautiful

 he quoted both

Aldous Huxley

 [10] and

Ananda Coomaraswamy

 [11] and he explained in

A Guide for the Perplexed

 that he had taken the term “the Reign of Quantity” from

René Guénon

 (

pictured

), [12] “one of the few significant metaphysicians of our time”. [13]


It was this aspect of Schumacher’s thinking which lay behind his judgement in the latter book, first published in 1977, that “while wealth may still be accumulating, the quality of man declines”. [14]


It also informed his criticism of the one-dimensionality of modern thought, in contrast to the “three-dimensional structure” of traditional wisdom. [15]


Contemporary society rejects ideas of “higher” or “lower” degrees of quality in favour of judgements based purely on quantity, he pointed out.


And yet the idea of something being “higher” is almost universally used in traditional ways of thinking across the world, he said: “‘Higher’ always means and implies ‘more inner’, ‘more interior’, ‘deeper’, ‘more intimate’; while ‘lower’ means and implies ‘more outer’, ‘more external’, ‘shallower’, ‘less intimate’. This synonymity can be found in many languages, perhaps in all of them”. [16]


It is also at the root of our ethical judgements, which regard good as being a “higher” quality than evil, argued Schumacher.


He observed: “The modern world tends to be sceptical about everything that demands man’s higher faculties. But it is not at all sceptical about scepticism, which demands hardly anything”. [17]


A Guide for the Perplexed

 is refreshingly clear about the obvious dead-end represented by the industrial monstrosity we are told is “civilization”.


Schumacher writes: “The faith in modern man’s omnipotence is wearing thin. Even if all the ‘new’ problems were solved by technological fixes, the state of futility, disorder and corruption would remain. It existed before the present crises became acute, and it will not go away by itself. More and more people are beginning to realise that ‘the modern experiment’ has failed”. [18]


Troy Southgate, whose fascinating political journey I recently

described

, [19] takes a close look at Schumacher’s philosophy through the lens of this particular work in his 2025 book

The World According to Fritz: E.F. Schumacher and The Perennial …

author: Unknown
title: Madenciler yine yollarda
content:
Manisa - Soma’da İmbat Madencilik şirketinin işçileri bir yıllık ücretlerinin ödenmemesi üzerine haklarını alamadıkları için Ankara’ya yürüme kararı aldı. Bu, madencilerin ilk yola çıkmaları değil. 1991 yılında Zonguldak maden işçileri, 100 bin kişiyi de yanlarına alarak tarih yazdılar. Toplu iş sözleşmesi (TİS) görüşmelerinde yaşanan anlaşmazlıklar, düşük ücretler, ödenmeyen maaşlar, özelleştirme girişimleri ve hükümetin uzlaşmaz tutumu ayağa kaldırmıştı madencileri.

Son yıllarda; Uyar Madencilik, Fernas Madencilik ve Doruk Madencilik işçileri de benzer gerekçelerle Ankara’nın yolunu tuttular. Güvenlik güçleri tarafından yolları kesildi gaz yediler, gözaltılar, tutuklamalar oldu ancak hiçbir şey yollarından döndüremedi onları. Ankara’da Kurtuluş parkını mesken tuttular, direndiler ve kısmen de olsa kazandılar.

O madenciler, yerin metrelerce altında zifiri karanlıklarda daracık dehlizlerde, havasız bacalarda ölümüne çalıştırılıp analarının ak sütü gibi helal olan hakları için yollara düşüyor. İnsanlık tarihi boyunca verilen mücadelelerle alınan en temel haklarını talep ediyor. İş, güvencesi, iş güvenliği ve çalışma koşullarının iyileştirilmesini istiyor. Kısaca insanca yaşam istiyor. Ancak karşılarında her sefer kolluk güçlerini buluyorlar. Eylemler uzayınca devletin üst düzey yetkilileriyle görüştürülüyor ve tutulmayan sözler verilerek geri çevriliyorlar. Sıcacık koltuklarında devletin her türlü olanağını kullananlar madencinin çalışma koşullarını, yaşadıklarını bilmedikleri için çözüm için adım atamamakta sadece aldıkları emirleri uygulamaktalar.

Madenciler, ekmekleri için sadece alın teri akıtmayıp canlarını da feda etmekteler. Son yirmi yılda binlerce maden emekçisi hayatlarının baharında yaşama veda ettiler. Soma’da 301 işçi zehirli gazdan nefessiz kalarak öldü. Tarihteki gaz odalarının vahşetini hatırlatan manzaralar yaşandı, bir damla kan akmadan can verdi gençlerimiz. Görünen kan, bir suçlu arar. Görünen kan, unutulmaz. Soma'da da kan görülmedi ve unutuldu yaşanan vahşet.

Ermenek’te maden ocağında kirli sularda nefessiz kaldı, boğuldu madenciler. ‘Benim oğlum yüzme bilmezdi’ diyen bir ananın feryatları kayboldu katı vicdanların labirentlerinde. Elbistan’da milyonlarca ton toprağın altında kaldı canlı bedenler, hala oradalar, çıkarılamadılar. Amasra’da, Karadon’da, Dursunbey’de grizu patlamasıyla iki bin derece sıcaklıkta yandı, kavruldu taze bedenler. Bunlara benzer onlarca olayda yüzlerce hayat söndü, hikayeler çok acı bitti.

Neyin bedeliydi bu acılar, yıkımlar. Egemenlerin, sermayedarların rahat yaşaması için birilerinin bedel ödemesi gerekiyordu. İşçi sağlığı ve iş güvenliği önlemlerini almak pahalı, yaşam ucuzdu bu ülkede. Cezasızlık ve hesap vermeme de alışkanlık olmuştu nasılsa.

Şimdi, bu acıları tekrar yaşamamak için yollara düşen madencilere müesses nizamın kurallarını uymadıkları için engel olunacaktır. “Aynı gemideyiz, ülkenin gerçekleri” gerekçeleriyle talepler ötelenecek ve sistem devam ettirilecektir. Ancak, asıl gerçekler madencilerin yaşadıklarıdır. Çözüm, o gerçekler üzerinden aranmalıdır. Madencilerin zor çalışma koşullarından kaynaklı direngenlikleri, zorlukları aşma becerileri ve mücadele azmi her türlü engeli aşacak, başarıyı getirecektir.

İşçilerin, emekçilerin sorunlarının çözümü için birlikte mücadele hayati önemdedir. Tarihte madenci direnişleri, ağır çalışma koşulları ve hayati riskler barındıran bir sektör olmasından dolayı işçi sınıfı mücadelesinin en sert ve kararlı eylemleri arasında yer almıştır.

Dünyada ve Türkiye'de bu direnişler, toplumsal yapılarda ve çalışma hukukunda köklü dönüşümler yaratmıştır. Küçük bir kıvılcım düşünceleri ve duyguları harekete geçiren büyük bir güç olabilir.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Maverick Avila
title: ‘Long fight ahead after ethanol spill in Tañon Strait’ – lawyer in landmark case
content:
Wastewater from an ethanol spill discolors Bais Bay, the Philippines’ Negros Oriental province, on Oct. 28, 2025, days after ethanol wastewater spilled into the bay, causing significant damage to coastal and marine ecosystems. Image courtesy of MarGale Bancairen.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX).

In 2007, Philippine environmental lawyer Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio and four other law professors in Cebu City sat around laughing at an idea: representing marine mammals in court.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX). The protected seascape between the islands of Cebu and Negros is home to 14 whale and dolphin species, as well as coral reefs and mangrove forests. The Japanese energy company performed seismic surveys and drilled an exploration well, which drove away dolphins and whales from the strait.

It was an ambitious plan, as animals had never been named as petitioners. Eisma-Osorio and fellow lawyer Golly Estenzo Ramos filed the first petition representing the resident marine mammals in December 2007. Their colleagues filed a second petition on behalf of fishing communities directly affected by the exploration activities.

The case, Resident Marine Mammals of the Protected Seascape Tañon Strait v. Secretary Angelo Reyes, went on for several years. In April 2015, the Philippine Supreme Court ruled to void the contract that allowed the exploration, development, and exploitation of petroleum resources within the Tañon Strait.

Eisma-Osorio joined Oceana Philippines as a consultant in 2015, a year after the NGO was established. At 56, she now leads the campaign and legal department as senior director of Oceana Philippines.

On October 24, 2025, a major ethanol wastewater spill hit Bais Bay, part of the Tañon Strait Protected Seascape (TSPS). Oceana Philippines collaborated with marine scientists to assess the severity of the spill. Their research, with the latest report in July this year, found that Universal Robina Corporation’s (URC) ethanol plant continued to leak wastewater, killing fish, corals and seagrass. The NGO is also consulting with fishing communities to build a court case against the company.

With more than 25 years of experience in natural resources law and policy, Eisma-Osorio believes it’s her personal responsibility to ensure there is legal accountability. In an interview with Mongabay via video call, she talked about representing marine mammals, the reaction from the community, and her current legal fight.

Mongabay: What was your thought process in deciding to represent the marine mammals in such a landmark case?

Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio: It was an ambitious undertaking. We wanted to challenge the thinking that only humans can file cases in court. And we knew there were two ways it could go: the court would throw out the case or decide to hear it. So we wanted to be sure, and we had Attorney Ramos and myself to act as stewards representing the marine mammals.

If you look at the case caption, the marine mammals were joined and represented by us, meaning they were also signing as individuals while being represented by us, because if the court did not allow them to join as litigants, it could still allow us to represent the dolphins and whales.

Mongabay: How was the case received back then, by communities, environmental groups, and even the court?

Eisma-Osorio: Around that time, what was refreshing about the campaign was that there was already an organic movement, especially the Save Tañon Strait Movement. There were very active Cebuanos, individuals, and students who helped raise awareness. The fisherfolk we represented were part of it too, so there was community engagement, because we knew they were the injured party in a way.

That was also the strategy behind two petitions. In the Philippines, you have to suffer an injury for the court to say you’re entitled to the remedy. We wanted the fisherfolk to prove their reduced catch and be heard, in the event that the court did not listen to the resident marine mammals case, since proof of injury was still a big question mark at that time.

Mongabay: At what point did you say, ‘This case is winnable?’ What was the turning point in lobbying to represent the resident marine mammals, especially with court updates? …

author: Kodao Productions
title: The Banwaon children of Balit
content:
This story was originally published in March 2015 that won first place in the photojournalism category of the

3rd Gawad Agong Para sa Pamamahayag

 and was a finalist in the inaugural

European Union Peace Journalism Awards

 in the same year.


Kodao is republishing this because it was lost in 2017 due to a website crash following a massive cyberattack.


= = = = =


Text and photos by Raymund B. Villanueva


They do not smile as often as other children.


They tell their visitors about the two-day trek from their forest communities under direct sun and drenching rain last January. They say they have never walked as far before. There were hardly roads in the 14 sitios (sub-villages) where they came from. A thousand of them belonging to 174 families left in a hurry, afraid of the lowlanders who came to their communities bearing big guns and wearing menacing scowls.


Their parents explained to them they had to leave their forest and mountain homes to survive. They are being killed for refusing excavations on their ancestral territory said to be rich in gold, copper, manganese, bromite and magnetite. The land that has nurtured them suddenly meant harm, as the strangers will kill them if they are not allowed to dig. Who among them knew that the land that bore them sweet potatoes and cassavas had so many metals they hardly heard of before?


An abandoned hospital compound is their temporary refuge here in Barangay Balit, San Luis, Agusan del Sur. It is unbearably hot during daytime and bitingly cold at night. Their parents had to construct small huts so each family would have their own space and somehow stem the spread of diseases. But the few trees around the compound could not afford them the play space they enjoyed back home.


There is never enough food to eat at this shelter, a situation they never experienced before. The land they temporarily left behind has always provided them with enough crops and fruits to eat. And if their Diwata (goddess) was in a good mood, they are provided with meat from the surrounding forests. Here, their mothers have stopped lactating due to want of food and four children have already died to common ailments worsened by severe under-nutrition.


They also fall ill due to lack of toilets and other hygiene facilities. Drinking water had to be fetched from some distance away, passing through a camp of soldiers who follow them around with their guns. They would often go without water rather than be anywhere nearer those mean men.


Some of them still find ways to play though. But many could not join in, as they are weak. Instead, they just look at those still strong enough to run around.


No, the Banwaon children in Barangay Balit do not smile as often as other children. Like children of other indigenous tribes throughout the Philippines they suffer from the persecutions by soldiers of the government. They are uprooted from their homes and vast playgrounds. They are denied food, education, medical care and safety.


But they come to life when they are asked to show how their elders hunted for food in their forests. Their limbs are energized when they perform plays to show how their people resist aggression from strangers. They find their voices when they sing songs of struggle and hope, songs about being back in their forests and mountain communities, free to run around and play, to fetch water for their mothers. They are as brave and heroic as their elders in the defense of their rights, beliefs and way of life.


As the International Solidarity Mission was preparing to leave the refugee center, some of the children milled around the kindly nuns who often visit them. It seemed they were saying they will carry on, that they are as steadfast as their elders in refusing mining and logging activities on their ancestral land.


When the vehicles carrying the nuns rounded the bend that led outside Barangay Balit, some of the children climbed the posts of the chicken-wire fence that enclosed the refugee center. Perhaps they were imagining they were up on some tree branch back in their villages, waving goodbyes to the wimpled angels sent to them by their Diwata to assure them there will be justice soon.


They were smiling. #


 


The post

The Banwaon children of Balit

 appeared first on

Kodao Productions

.

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: California’s New Balcony Solar Bill Isn’t a Victory — It’s a Compromise
content:
Plug-in balcony solar panels can never match the booming rooftop solar movement that state utility regulators derailed.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

California Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed SB 868, a bill legalizing residential solar panels for balconies. At a time when the Trump administration is unraveling federal climate progress, California’s so-called “Plug and Play Solar Act” enables homeowners and renters to purchase and plug lightweight solar panels into a regular power outlet and generate up to 1200 watts of electricity. While environmentalists are hailing the bill as a major step toward mitigating climate change, balcony solar is a mere consolation prize in comparison to rooftop solar, which could have made solar power ubiquitous in the nation’s most populous state if it hadn’t been derailed by the state government in order to protect private utilities’ profits.

Joshua Frank, co-author of the new book, Bad Energy: The AI Hucksters, Rogue Lithium Extractors, and Wind Industrialists Who Are Selling Off Our Future, explained in an interview that “for those who have lived in California for over the last 15, 20 years, there was a heyday for rooftop solar.” Frank added: “You could walk anywhere, and someone was trying to tell you, you can buy rooftop solar,” because there was a “big solar boom happening in the state” as a result of public subsidies.

The idea of generating power right where it’s most needed is an ideal solution to help stabilize a warming climate. With the cost of solar panel technology falling dramatically, all that is needed is for governments to incentivize the public to adopt solar power. According to Environment America, that looks like “supportive public policies that make it convenient, fast and affordable to install solar panels,” including rebates and tax credits, and “rules such as ‘net metering’ that assure fair and adequate compensation for the extra solar power that panel owners send to the grid.”

Starting in the mid-2000s, California did just that, doubling down every few years to offer stronger inducements for residents to adopt solar technology. “People were putting rooftop solar with government subsidies on their roofs, and it was fantastic,” said Frank. “We were actually setting the standard of what you can do to combat climate change on the solar level.” As rooftop solar became more popular, there were dreams of a wave of green energy jobs buoying the state’s economy.

But there was one problem that climate justice advocates hadn’t counted on: the falling corporate profits of utilities companies like Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), which were making money from building out the transmission grid rather than selling electricity to consumers. Bernadette Del Chiaro, a senior vice president with the Environmental Working Group in California, said: “These utility companies are essentially construction companies. They make money off of building all of those transmission lines, so they’re constantly pushing to have power plants located really far away from where we all live and work so that we’re dependent on them.”

By 2023, rooftop solar installations in California fell by 80 percent, not because residents were less interested in the technology, but because the state utilities regulators weakened incentives such as the Net Energy Metering (NEM) system that made the technology financially attractive to cash-strapped Californians.

Frank blames Newsom, whose ties to PG&E go back to his years as mayor of San Francisco. The company heavily lobbied Newsom and other influential voices against rooftop solar. The result, according to Frank, was enormous pressure to “essentially gut this rooftop solar program, and at the same time, open up public lands for massive solar development.”

To protect its profits from the booming rooftop solar industry, PG&E claimed that California’s NEM plan was unfair to low-income people of color because it rewarded homeowners who benefitted from rooftop solar while shifting the burden of maintaining the grid to those who couldn’t afford it. “They hired a fancy PR firm,” said Del Chiaro, “and they cooked up this whole story about how rooftop solar was bad for poor people, and it was the reason why electricity rates were going up in California.”

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Farmers, fisherfolk demand urgent aid amid El Niño, rising fuel prices
content:
The absence of reliable irrigation makes it difficult for farmers to continue planting during periods of extreme heat.


By Wendyl Geronimo

Davao Today


From drought-stricken farms in Davao and Nueva Ecija to fishing communities in Albay, farmers and fisherfolk are demanding government assistance, protection against land grabbing and genuine agrarian reform as El Niño, mounting production costs and development projects threaten their livelihoods.


Amid worsening agricultural conditions, rising production expenses and continuing disputes over land ownership, farmers and fisherfolk across the Philippines are calling for immediate government intervention, warning that insufficient assistance and threats of displacement are pushing rural communities deeper into poverty.


Their demands come as agricultural communities confront the effects of El Niño, inadequate irrigation systems, expensive fuel and fertilizer, and development projects that farmers organizations say threaten thousands of hectares of farmland.


In the Davao Region, prolonged dry conditions have affected agricultural production, particularly among farmers dependent on rainfall.


Approximately P410 million in agricultural losses were recorded in the Davao region due to El Niño.


Enalyn Basarte, president of the Masupil Women Farmers Organization in Lamanan, Calinan, Davao City, described how insufficient rainfall damaged their corn and vegetable crops.


“Our squash did not flower and the corn was very small and did not form ears,” Basarte told

Davao Today

in Cebuano.


The experience highlights the difficulties faced by small farmers whose livelihoods depend on increasingly unpredictable weather conditions.


The Davao City Agriculturist’s Office also reported preparations to address the effects of El Niño, including the deployment of water pumps, water tankers and other agricultural equipment. The city government said approximately 700 rainwater catchment units had been established in upland communities.


Despite these measures, farmers’ experiences across the country underscore the continuing need for accessible irrigation, production subsidies and agricultural assistance.


Farmers struggle with inadequate irrigation and government assistance


For Neneng Aquino, a farmer from San Isidro, Nueva Ecija, the struggle to sustain agricultural production has become increasingly difficult because of inadequate irrigation facilities, rising production costs and insufficient government support.


Aquino said farmers in her community depend primarily on rainfall, leaving their crops vulnerable to prolonged dry spells.


“We are happy that we are able to plant there even if it’s just for seasoning. What’s not good is that the assistance we are asking for from the DA, it’s not enough, it’s not being received,” Aquino told

Davao Today

in an interview.


She explained that the absence of reliable irrigation makes it difficult for farmers to continue planting during periods of extreme heat.


“We only have rain. We won’t be able to survive if it’s too dry,” she added.


She also said that their income is insufficient to sustain their daily needs.


Apart from the threat of drought, she pointed to the increasing cost of fertilizer and pesticides, alongside the limited bargaining power of farmers when selling their produce.


“In fertilizer, they are the ones who decide the price. We will pay them the amount they want,” Aquino said. “But for us, our farmers, the negotiators will decide how much they want to buy.”


The situation leaves farmers struggling to recover their production expenses while earning enough to support their families.


Aquino emphasized the need for agricultural equipment and improved irrigation facilities.


“If possible, we need a tractor and a water pump. We need a water pump so that the water will be continuous,” she said.


However, she said farmers had yet to receive sufficient assistance to prepare for the effects of El Niño.


“We are still requesting [for support]. That’s why we don’t know what their plans are for us,” Aquino added.


Beyond the lack of agricultural support, Aquino also raised concerns about disputes over the land they cultivate.


She recalled an incident in which an unidentified individual prevented farmers from working on their farmland.


“When we plow the land, someone forbade us to plow the land,” she said. “We don’t know who he is, but he forbade us to plow the land.”

author: Justin Nobel
title: Ohio Denies Evidence of Fracking Waste in Drinking Water. Its Own Records Show Otherwise.
content:
This story was co-published with Rolling Stone.


In Ohio’s rural southeastern corner, Marietta College geology professor David Jeffrey was among the residents worried that industry activity in America’s booming natural gas region could be polluting their drinking water. That’s “the biggest fear,” he said at an August meeting with top Ohio officials.


When Jeffrey and residents from advocacy groups Buckeye Environmental Network and Washington County for Safe Drinking Water met with Ohio officials, those state officials repeatedly assured residents that despite the up to 1.4 billion gallons of oil and gas wastewater injected in underground wells in their county and across Ohio each year, the state was unaware of any resulting drinking water contamination there.


“We would have heard about it,” Mary Mertz, director of the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR), which oversees both aspects of Ohio’s environment and its oil and gas industry, told residents in the August 17 virtual meeting.


“No one has called us that I’m aware of,” said Eric Vendel, ODNR’s oil and gas division chief. “We have a water investigation form that can be filled out and we would have my team down there and investigate the water.”


What officials did not tell the group that day is that five years earlier, the state did receive a call and, on Vendel’s orders, investigated a drinking water well for oil and gas wastewater contaminants in eastern Ohio, roughly 80 miles away from Washington County. Independent experts say the results are consistent with fracking wastewater contamination. Despite that and the water well’s location

near two oil and gas wastewater injection wells

, ODNR concluded fracking wastewater was not to blame, according to documents DeSmog and

Rolling Stone

Concerns over polluted drinking water cross political and social divides, perhaps nowhere more so than rural Washington County. As intensely salty wastewater pushed below ground resurfaces, residents and officials have injected the issue into the already bitterly divided Ohio governor’s race. Susan Vessels, a Republican official in Washington County, recently appeared alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton because of Acton’s pledge to pause new wastewater wells in this densely drilled area. “We have a chance to prevent the worst from happening, and we need to act now,” Acton told DeSmog and

Rolling Stone

.


“Drinking water is not political and it is my hope Ohioans will come together across party lines on this issue.”

Susan Vessels, Marietta City Council President


Ohio ranks in the

top 10 nationally

 for both oil and gas production. Fracking can occur within 100 feet of a school or rural home, and operators have been able to tap the gas-rich Marcellus and Utica formations by drilling directly beneath water reservoirs and state parks. But in order to maintain that production, the industry has to offload the tidal wave of toxic wastewater — rich in salts, carcinogens, heavy metals, and radioactive elements — that surfaces in the weeks and years that follow drilling an oil or gas well.


That wastewater gets pumped into injection wells deep below ground, where impermeable geological layers are supposed to keep it from leaking into oil and gas wells or drinking water supplies. Washington County, whose 19 injection wells

outnumber all of Pennsylvania

, has received complaints of this wastewater, or brine,

flooding nearby oil and gas wells

, according to the New York Times.


Now, an hour and a half drive north, in the town of Coshocton, Ohio, records show evidence of a family’s drinking water polluted by high levels of the same types of salts found in fracking wastewater.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
content:
British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he also warned of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.


Doerkson made the comments as newly elected Conservatives gathered for their first caucus meeting on Monday, where he told them that their job now is to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.


He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.


“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”


He said that B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every single time.


Doerkson said people will be watching to see if his caucus will splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.


“I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can hold it together,” he said.


“So, let me save everyone the suspense: this caucus is unified,” Doerkson said to cheers from the crowd.


Conservative members quit or were fired from the caucus just months into Findlay’s leadership before she resigned two days before the NDP under David Eby set off an election.


The members came back after Doerkson was appointed and he led the party to the election win.


Doerkson said B.C. residents can count on the Conservatives to stay focused on what they were elected to do.


He said a Conservative government will deliver a better economy, health care system and public safety.


“That is what we are going to do, and it is absolutely my intention to do it as quickly as possible,” he said.


The incoming premier says legislators will be sworn on Nov. 19 and the new cabinet will be announced on Nov. 20.


Doerkson did not say whether he would recall the legislature for a fall session, but repeated previous promises made on the campaign trail.


“That means putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working British Columbians,” he said. “It means treating taxpayers with respect and saying no to new taxes. It means giving small businesses room to grow with a (provincial sales tax) exemption that will help them to invest, hire and succeed.”


Doerkson also said his government would repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, while continuing to “build strong relationships” with First Nations in the province.


“I am committed that we will do that also as soon as we can,” he said.


First Nations chiefs in B.C. have warned against repealing the legislation, urging instead to use it as a framework for reconciliation.


Doerkson also signalled a change in housing legislation.


“We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria.”


The post

Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says

 appeared first on

APTN News

title: Todos Santos en Flores: años de organización comunitaria frente a las restricciones a las ceremonias andinas
content:
Foto: vidal Arnaldo – Cementerio de Flores


La celebración del Aya Mark’ay Quilla en el Cementerio de Flores llega al 2 de noviembre de 2026 con nuevos acuerdos para el ingreso de ofrendas, instrumentos musicales y elementos propios de las prácticas ancestrales andino-amazónicas. Detrás de estas medidas existe un proceso de organización impulsado por familias, músicos y referentes de pueblos originarios que denuncian años de restricciones y controles policiales. Las comunidades advierten que la disputa por el reconocimiento de sus prácticas espirituales continúa en otros espacios públicos de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.

Por Mario Canaviri (ANRed).


Durante años, las comunidades andinas que se reúnen cada 2 de noviembre en el Cementerio de Flores denunciaron requisas, retención de ofrendas y restricciones al ingreso de instrumentos musicales y otros elementos de sus ceremonias. En 2026, la Mesa del Aya Mark’ay Quilla anunció nuevos acuerdos con autoridades del Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, resultado de un proceso de organización que sus protagonistas consideran fundamental para ejercer sus derechos culturales y espirituales.


El Aya Mark’ay Quilla, conocido también como Todos Santos, es una práctica ancestral que reúne a las familias para recibir y despedir a sus difuntos. En los hogares se preparan mesas con alimentos, flores, t’antawawas —panes tradicionales— y objetos vinculados con la memoria de quienes fallecieron. El 2 de noviembre, parte de esas ofrendas se lleva a los cementerios para compartirlas con otras familias y comunidades, en un encuentro de reciprocidad.


foto todo santos – 2018 fotografia maria pomacusi con el sikuri daniel – reinaldo ortega


María Pomacusi, mujer originaria quechua e integrante del proceso organizativo, sitúa alrededor de 2006 el comienzo de un período de mayores restricciones institucionales. Según su reconstrucción, hacia 2010 se intensificó la presencia de fuerzas de seguridad en los accesos al cementerio, con controles que dificultaban el desarrollo de las ceremonias. La referente cuestiona que estas prácticas sean tratadas como costumbres extranjeras, cuando forman parte de la vida de pueblos y naciones anteriores a la conformación de los Estados actuales y mantienen una fuerte presencia entre las familias del Bajo Flores y otros barrios porteños.


De las restricciones a la organización comunitaria


En 2017, Pomacusi comenzó a involucrarse en la organización a partir de los relatos que acercó Daniel Paz, integrante del movimiento de sikuris, sobre las situaciones que atravesaban las familias. Ante esas denuncias, un grupo de músicos impulsó una intervención pacífica en las puertas del cementerio para acompañar a las comunidades, visibilizar las restricciones y registrar lo que ocurría durante la jornada.En ese proceso, el trabajo de documentación realizado por el fotógrafo Reinaldo Ortega, cuyos registros permitieron recuperar imágenes de celebraciones anteriores. Para la referente, esas fotografías constituyen una parte importante de la memoria colectiva sobre las condiciones en las que se desarrollaba el Aya Mark’ay Quilla antes de las restricciones denunciadas. 


foto reinaldo ortega 2019 – represión 1


Con la colaboración de Elisa Suárez, referente territorial de la Comuna 7, establecieron contactos con autoridades policiales y espacios de seguridad. Tras presentar notas y mantener reuniones, pudieron realizar la intervención, aunque Pomacusi recuerda momentos de tensión con las fuerzas de seguridad. La experiencia permitió recoger testimonios y documentar situaciones como la retención de t’antawawas y otros elementos. También resultaron importantes los registros fotográficos de Reinaldo Ortega, que ayudaron a reconstruir antecedentes de las celebraciones.


A partir de 2018, las comunidades profundizaron la búsqueda de interlocutores institucionales y convocaron a organizaciones sociales e indígenas para acompañar sus reclamos. La organización comenzó a consolidar una Mesa de Trabajo que, con la participación de distintos espacios a lo largo de los años, sostuvo gestiones ante autoridades del Gobierno porteño, responsables del cementerio y representantes comunales.


Para Pomacusi, el conflicto no se limitaba a los controles de ingreso. También cuestionaba una interpretación institucional que pretendía reducir las ceremonias andinas a llevar flores y realizar una oración, desplazando las ofrendas y otras expresiones ancestrales. La referente advierte que …

author: Joseph Lee
title: DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects
content:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.


The community relies on diesel for 75 percent of its power, and residents put about 20 percent of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the

average energy burden

 for low-income households nationwide. 


“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”


That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions. 


But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused. 


That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and

underinvestment in Indigenous communities

. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while

DOGE eliminated another $468 million

, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs. 


According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the

federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes

, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.


Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment. 


“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”


The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the

Hopi Tribe

 was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut. 


Kotzebue, Alaska, is accessible only by air and sea, and most of its fuel arrives in a three-month window before sea ice makes it difficult for ships to arrive.


Prisma Bildagentur / Universal Images Group via Getty Images


Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

author: Mavic Conde
title: UN raises standard for IP consent
content:
Photo courtesy of Marcelino Tena

“This is reasonable, provided that what the guidance says is followed in practice.”

The United Nations stressed this point in its new guidance on the free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) for business projects affecting Indigenous Peoples territories.

The guidance, issued by the UN Human Rights Council in June, states that governments should seek and obtain FPIC before granting licenses or concessions within ancestral domains. They must also ensure that Indigenous Peoples’ rights are respected, including when decisions need a longer time or a reassessment.

It stresses that consent is “not a one-time event but an ongoing process.” According to the report, Indigenous Peoples have the right to reconsider their decisions if circumstances change, agreed conditions are not fulfilled, or new information emerges about the project’s impact. They may also decline to participate if they believe consultations are not being conducted in good faith or need more time and resources to strengthen their institutions.

The guidance addresses recurring concerns of governments conducting consultations only after having granted key approvals and failure to recognize that consent is “dynamic and iterative in nature.”

These gaps in implementation have “caused conflicts, resulted in harm, and triggered cycles of violence confronting States and businesses with Indigenous Peoples,” the report said.

“I believe this is reasonable, provided that what the guidance says is followed in practice.” Marcelino Tena, a Dumagat-Remontado Indigenous leader, said in Filipino in a virtual interview with Bulatlat.

Tena was among those who challenged the consultation process for the Kaliwa Dam project in Quezon and Rizal provinces, arguing that it failed to reflect community opposition and adequately represent their decisions.

The UN guidance came a month after the Philippine National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) approved the revised 2012 FPIC guidelines. Recognized under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), FPIC is intended to ensure that Indigenous communities can make informed decisions about projects affecting their territories.

The revised guidelines classify projects into Category A, B, and C, with different consent procedures. Categories A and B require FPIC through customary decision-making processes while Category C projects such as community-driven, non-commercial, and many government-funded projects may proceed with a shortened validation instead of the full procedure.

The changes have drawn criticism from human rights advocates, including the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center (LRC). In a briefer, the non-profit cultural research organization described the 2026 framework a critical departure from the 2012 guidelines, stressing that it “strips away the vital safeguard of community oversight.”

“Characterizing [redacted] projects as Category C merely because they are government-funded and non-commercial fails to account for their actual impacts on Indigenous communities and their ancestral domains,” the LRC said.

The organization warned that compressed timelines could affect meaningful participation, as internal consultations take time and attending meetings often requires days of travel on foot.

In a statement, the Human Rights Watch said that while the declaration is not a binding treaty, the Philippines supported its adoption by the UN General Assembly in 2007.

The NCIP initially acknowledged Bulatlat’s request for comment but has not yet provided a response.

Tena said that his community completed and submitted its Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plan (ADSDPP) to the NCIP in September. The plan guides the protection and governance of their ancestral domain under customary laws. He said that the plan and their certificate of ancestral land domain title (CADT) cannot exist without the other. The community obtained its CADT in 2008 but developing the plan took nearly two decades.

In a Facebook post, Tena acknowledged disagreements during the process which he said were necessary to identify and support the community’s collective will.

The Philippines is among the countries the UN Working Group cited as having laws requiring consultation with IPs. But the report warns that legal recognition alone does not guarantee effective implementation of the FPIC. For companies and …

title: Ableistisches journalistisches Versagen
content: Dieser wurde aber weitgehend totgeschwiegen. Es gab kaum Presseberichte. Selbst über die Besetzung eines Bundesministeriums berichtete einzig die Frankfurter Rundschau. Journalist*innen schreiben lieber über Einzelschicksale. Mitleid-erweckende Berichte generieren online Klicks und gefallen Leser*innen. Die Berichte bleiben oberflächlich und die systemischen und politischen Hintergründe werden nicht beleuchtet. Betroffene als Objekte einer bequemen Berichtserstattung. Sobald Betroffene als Akteur*innen auftreten und das System, das sie behindert, anprangern, werden sie unsichtbar gemacht. Die Redaktionen stehen offenbar zu dieser ableistischen Linie. Der Lüneburger Behindertenbeirat kritisierte die Nicht-Berichtserstattung der Landeszeitung (LZ) über eine Kundgebung am europäischen Protesttag für die Gleichstellung von Menschen mit Behinderung. Die Redaktion antwortete am 22. Mai 2026 wie folgt: „Anm. d. Red.: Am Protesttag selbst hat die LZ tatsächlich nicht berichtet. Wir stellen hingegen regelmäßig Schicksale von Menschen mit Einschränkungen in den Mittelpunkt von Geschichten – unabhängig von Protest- oder Gedenktagen. So haben wir beispielsweise am 9. Mai von der 16-jährigen Lotti berichtet, die trotz Unterstützungsbedarf ihren Traumberuf lernen will.“ Selbst die verwendete Sprache ist hier ableistisch. Das Wort „Behinderung“ wird gemieden, obwohl dies kein Schimpfwort ist, sondern eine neutrale Eigenschaft. Das ist ein journalistisches Versagen. Die Graswurzelrevolution wird dagegen über die Proteste und ihre Hintergründe ausführlich in der GWR 514 berichten. Seid auf den Schwerpunkt der Dezemberausgabe gespannt!

author: Sarah Hughes
title: Members Alarmed by End-Run around Democracy at Buffalo Health Care Local
content:
Things had been tense for some time inside the leadership of Communications Workers (CWA) Local 1168, a 4,800-member health care union based near Buffalo, New York. Still, it was a high-functioning local with a busy calendar of events, stewards handling grievances, organizers pursuing leads, and leaders organizing at work.


So it was a surprise to members in June when their parent union, CWA, put the local into trusteeship, at the request of the local’s president and seven of the nineteen executive board members.


Trusteeship meant the union’s bylaws and elected leaders were suspended, and most of its work temporarily ground to a halt. The appointed Director of Organizing and Mobilizing Mary Nowocien and elected Vice President Patrick Weisansal II found themselves locked out of their group chats, email, and union hall, and facing an internal union prosecution.


A staffer of CWA District 1, Erin Spaulding, was assigned as trustee—tasked with maintaining the functioning of the local, setting up and overseeing judicial processes for the charges against officers, and making a plan to return the union to local control.


Nowocien and Weisansal saw the sudden trusteeship as an escalation of a long-running conflict and a deliberate undermining of the upcoming union elections. Weisansal had just announced his intention to run against incumbent President Cori Gambini.


Now the elections are on hold until the trials are over, whenever that is. And lately, the employer has been taking advantage of the turmoil in the union.


While the allegations are serious, members are concerned that the trusteeship was a nuclear option for an internal financial matter and that it has torn apart relationships at the local, weakened opposition to management’s schemes and denied democratic processes to an active, engaged union membership.


ALLEGED TIMECARD ISSUES


The trusteeship filing lists the cause as “serious allegations of financial misconduct” from officers and “dueling charges” between leaders.


Gambini and Executive Vice President Robert Andruszko had accused Nowocien and Weisansal of defrauding the local of thousands of dollars, by getting paid by both the union and their employer for the same hours worked, and by falsifying records. These issues came to light during a timecard audit in the fall of 2025 by their employer, Kaleida Health.


Nowocien and Weisansal acknowledged there were significant errors on old timecards and paychecks, but said it was the product of the employer’s faulty timekeeping and payroll system, and human error. The majority of other officers also had issues, they pointed out, but only some were being singled out for discipline by the local and the employer.


Spaulding, the trustee, interviewed all the suspended officers and allowed the majority to return to their paid positions—with the exception of Nowocien, Weisansal, and three others not facing any charges: the Communications and Political Directors and one of the Area Vice Presidents. Also fired were two longtime staff organizers, on the grounds that there was no work for them to do, according to one, Ann Converso, who had recently helped organize a new unit of substance use disorder counselors and was gearing up for their first contract fight.


Many current leaders on both sides of this schism were part of a reform caucus in Local 1168, the Caucus of Rank-and-File Healthcare Employees (CORHE), which dissolved when they won their positions in 2020.


Since winning, Gambini and a few others have butted heads with Weisansal, Nowocien, and others over how to tackle problems. The latter camp frequently organized their facility—Buffalo General Hospital, the union’s largest unit—to push back against management’s changes and violations. Gambini and leaders aligned with her argued that that wasn’t the right approach—that they had to pick their fights and not overextend the membership, according to Weisansal.


One Buffalo General steward, who asked to not be named, said members were appalled that the trustee had removed elected officers. “If our employer treated one of our members in a similar fashion,” the steward said, “union leadership would rally around them and fight to return them to their position!”


Spaulding wrote in a public FAQ posted on the local’s social media that the temporary administration “is not intended to be punitive or find guilt against any individual in the Local. It is intended to stabilize the Local while issues are …

author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Across Asia and the Pacific, 350 million women and girls with disabilities navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making.

To break down these barriers, Women Enabled International (WEI) and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific have officially launched a landmark publication today: the Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society.

Read the full Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: “Nothing about us without us”.

As WEI Executive Director Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana stated during the launch:

“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”

UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, Christine Arab, added:

“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”

The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance.

The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all four WPS pillars:

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

The guide also features a practical Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation.

This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the Government of the Republic of Korea (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project “Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”, and of the Australian Government under the Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies (2023–2027).
